articles.title_orig: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
articles.title_zh: China-linked network using AI fakes to smear Taiwan election candidates, BBC Verify finds
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan's ruling party is being repeatedly targeted with AI videos spreading false claims about its leader and other key members ahead of crucial local elections, BBC Verify has found.
A China-linked network has pumped out more than 500 fake videos about the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) in the past year, which experts suggest is part of a long-running campaign to influence the outcome of the elections.
The videos appear to try to smear President Lai Ching-te by claiming he holds a US green card - and would abandon Taiwan if war broke out with China - which Taiwan's presidential office says is completely false. Deepfakes also appear to show Puma Shen, who is running to be the mayor of capital Taipei, using drugs, which he denies. Others seek to undermine or ridicule the politicians by showing them in children's clothing or as popular film characters.
The Taipei mayoralty has traditionally served as a springboard to the presidency. Experts say this has made Shen, who has been openly critical of Beijing, an obvious target for disinformation campaigns. The current mayor, Chiang Wan-an, is part of Taiwan's Kuomintang (KMT) party, which favours closer ties with China.
Taiwan is a self-governing island that China claims as part of its territory. Beijing and Taipei have long observed an uneasy status quo under which Taiwan, backed by the US, neither formally declares independence nor unites with China.
But tensions have risen since the DPP came to power in 2016. Beijing has repeatedly accused the party of pursuing independence while China's leader Xi Jinping, who has said "reunification" with Taiwan is a key goal, has stepped up pressure against the party with increased military activity around the island.
Experts believe the current disinformation activity is part of a broader campaign against Taiwan designed to undermine trust in its democratic process.
"The account operators are trying to make people distrust the DPP politicians so that they will not believe whatever they say," Austin Horng-En Wang, an expert in cognitive warfare at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, told BBC Verify. "If you don't trust that candidate then you will not listen to what they say," he added.
The videos, many of which were shared from an account called "noxparable" or carried a watermark with the same name, have been viewed tens of millions of times across several social media platforms since May 2025.
More than half of those views were tracked in the past four months as the activity has ramped up ahead of the elections. Many of the accounts involved in spreading disinformation listed their locations on social media as mainland China and Hong Kong, while a number of the clips carried labels showing they were generated with AI. Many people who engaged with the videos were often seen repeating the false claims or attacking DPP figures in the comments, while others appeared to treat the clips as entertainment.
One of the most widely shared videos targeted Shen by superimposing his face onto a man who is seen holding a lighter and exhaling smoke alongside claims he is smoking drugs. The video appears to build on accusations from Taiwan's opposition party that he supports drugs decriminalisation, which Shen denies, and was debunked by a local news network.
Shen has taken legal action against people sharing deepfakes, local media reported, while his campaign office said AI videos showing the candidate appeared to be part of a "classic tactic China uses to smear specific targets". BBC Verify contacted the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
Other debunked claims include allegations that Lai's predecessor Tsai Ing-wen had fraudulently obtained her PhD from the London School of Economics. The university pushed back on identical allegations in 2019 and confirmed it had awarded her the doctorate.
A number of the social media accounts BBC Verify identified as sharing the disinformation videos appeared to be linked to Chinese firm Borderless, which produces websites that blend apolitical content with pro-China messaging. The network has also been investigated by journalists at the Taiwanese independent media outlet The Reporter, who shared their findings with BBC Verify. Borderless has previously been accused of carrying out "cognitive warfare" against Taiwan by Taipei's National Security Bureau and the firm has been contacted for comment.
Analysts confirmed to BBC Verify there were also linguistic clues that the accounts, which presented themselves as based in Taiwan, were actually posting from China. The posts occasionally used a simplified Chinese script introduced by the Communist government which was never adopted in Taiwan.
The posts mostly appeared during regular office hours, which Wang suggested showed a "professional" operation, while the accounts originating outside Taiwan showed evidence of election interfering. "When they pretended to be citizens in another country and used these accounts to manipulate the public opinion of the other country during the campaign, it is definitely election interference," Wang added.
Earlier this month, Taiwan's central election commission aired an advert warning voters to "beware of AI-generated deepfake videos" circulating online that could seek to influence the upcoming election. It comes as government officials flagged nearly 2,700 social media accounts to Meta that it claimed were part of a Chinese information warfare campaign, Reuters reported. Meta said it had removed the accounts.
Andrew Yeh of the China Strategic Risk Institute said the ultimate goal is not to favour any party. "China's information operations succeed not just by backing one candidate or opposing another, but by diluting Taiwan's policy debates, driving polarisation and degrading Taiwanese citizens' trust in their democratic processes," he said.
"Regardless of whether the KMT or DPP comes out on top, a more fractured and more divided Taiwan is in Beijing's interests."

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says attack on Russian ships in Libya was self-defence
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones and the attack also targeted a second vessel, a cargo ship which was being used to transport weapons, Zelensky said.
Footage verified by the BBC shows a ship ablaze at Benghazi's port.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.

articles.title_orig: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets
articles.title_zh: Chinese tech giant Huawei convicted of federal charges, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets
articles.content_orig:
Chinese tech giant Huawei was convicted of multiple federal charges in New York Tuesday after prosecutors accused the company of stealing technology from U.S. companies, abusing the American financial system and helping Iran spy on its citizens.
A jury in New York’s Eastern District found the company guilty of seven conspiracy counts that included bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, defrauding the United States and conspiracy to steal trade secrets.
The company was also convicted of bank fraud and wire fraud. Huawei was acquitted of two counts, a racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to obstruct justice.
In a statement, Huawei said the charges are “without legal or factual merit” and it said it “welcomes” the racketeering verdict.
“We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the company said.
Huawei attorney Brian Heberling said the company plans to appeal. At sentencing, which is scheduled for Sept. 14, Huawei could face large fines and other penalties.
Prosecutors accused the company, which makes smartphones and has telecom networks around the world, of encouraging its workforce of 200,000 in 170 countries to lie, cheat, and steal “for a competitive advantage to grow and protect its business.”
Huawei was accused of misappropriating intellectual property like source code, user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology and robot testing technology, prosecutors said. The victims included Cisco Systems, Motorola Solutions, T-Mobile, Quintel USA and Fujitsu, according to the Associated Press.
In an interview Tuesday, Heberling rejected the government’s allegations, saying prosecutors presented a “caricature-like portrait” of Huawei of as a corrupt organization with company policies that condoned crime.
“That was just profoundly inconsistent with the company that I experienced in my work, but more importantly, [with] the evidence, which really showed a series of isolated events over a 20-year period,” he said. “No company can insure perfection over that period of time.”
Heberling argued that the racketeering acquittal — the most serious charge the company faced — showed a “profound rejection of the narrative the United States pursued in this case.”
Huawei was previously banned from selling equipment to U.S. carriers over fears that it poses a security risk, according to the Associated Press, and it was blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
Adam Reiss is a reporter and producer for NBC and MSNBC.
Tim Stelloh is a breaking news reporter for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees and Says He Is in Therapy
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees and Says He Is in Therapy
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang. She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.
In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.
And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.

articles.title_orig: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.title_zh: Beverly Hills plastic surgeon branded ‘magician’ over dramatic transformation of 61-year-old mom after $45K facelift
articles.content_orig:
Beauty is in the eye of the beholder.
But it seems that everyone was blown away by one woman’s recent facelift transformation .
Dr. Marc Levin, a facial plastic surgeon in Beverly Hills , specializes in “dramatic yet undetectable facial rejuvenation.”
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
The expert, 30, who became one of the youngest board-certified surgeons in North America, regularly shares images of his patients before and after their procedures.
Most recently, he uploaded snapshots of 61-year-old hairdresser Helen, who underwent a grueling nine-and-a-half-hour surgery — and the results left the internet stunned.
Dr. Levin shared in the caption of the post: “What a transformation! Absolutely no stone was left unturned for Helen. Every millimeter of her face was analyzed and appropriately addressed.”
He explained how her “character and beauty still remain,” adding: “She is just a younger-looking, more refreshed and clean version of herself.”
Speaking to the California Post, Dr. Levin dished further details about Helen’s “comprehensive facial rejuvenation plan,” which came with a $45,000 price tag.
The extensive list of procedures included an extended deep-plane face and neck lift, endoscopic brow lift, upper blepharoplasty, scarless lower blepharoplasty, facial fat grafting, CO2 laser and an earlobe reduction.
“I’m kind of a younger surgeon so I’m doing the most modern innovations, facial rejuvenation techniques and facelifting techniques,” he told The Post.
And his craftsmanship did not go unnoticed by social media users who flooded to the comments to offer praise.
“Absolutely beautiful… you are so talented and skilled,” one wrote, as another added: “Well, dang…that is a fabulous result!”
Others were quick to brand the surgeon a “magician” and “miracle worker” after seeing the finished results.
In a separate video, Helen, who is originally from South Africa, offered insight on how the procedure had changed her entire outlook.
She began by explaining that she had been “miserable” before taking the plunge to get surgery.
“I looked at the outside of myself and I thought, ‘Oh my God, what is happening to me over here?’ It didn’t match how I was feeling on the inside,” the mom said.
But now, three months post-surgery, she has found a new lease of life.
“I feel like I look like my daughter [now],” Helen revealed, adding: “Thank you for giving me the gift of confidence back.
“How fortunate am I to have the best and most caring surgeon. I’m just so grateful,” she concluded.
Dr. Levin explained that patients will start to see settled results within two to three weeks after surgery.
During this short time frame, “you are able to go out and nobody should know that you had surgery if you have your hair down and makeup on.”
He shared that patients would see their “final results” within three to four months, but will “continuously look better and better for 10 to 12 months after surgery.”

articles.title_orig: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.title_zh: Live storm updates: Record king tides leave Bay Area roads flooded
articles.content_orig:
Dangerous high tides, waves reaching up to 30 feet and an incoming storm are expected to bring flooding, heavy rain and strong winds to parts of Northern California this week, threatening coastal communities with road closures, erosion and dangerous beach conditions. The National Weather Service said Tuesday that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
LIVE: Track rain in San Francisco Bay Area with Live Doppler 7
Low-lying coastal areas could see flooded roads, road closures and erosion. Rising water and waves could also reach farther up beaches than usual, leaving people with fewer ways to escape.
Meanwhile, a cold front is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rain and gusty winds from Tuesday evening into Wednesday morning.
Coastal flood warnings will remain in effect in several areas through Wednesday and Thursday, depending on location.

Powerful king tides pushed San Francisco water levels above 8 feet on Tuesday morning, breaking a previous record for November set in 1982, the National Weather Service said.
At 10:06 a.m. Tuesday, the tidal gauge at Crissy Field near the Presidio was measured at 8.23 feet. The previous record was 7.97 feet on Nov 30 1982. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's tidal records for San Francisco date back to June 29, 1854.
More records could be set Wednesday morning, when the highest tides are expected, according to the weather service.
At the San Francisco tide gauge, water levels could reach 8.5 feet, or 2.7 feet above normal, at 10:49 a.m. In Monterey, tides could rise to 8.4 feet, or 3 feet above normal, at 9:39 a.m., forecasters said.
Early Tuesday, the weather service said that coastal flooding could reach major to extreme levels in some areas as unusually high tides combine with storm-driven ocean surges.
The City of San Francisco has released a storm and flood hazard map that shows which areas are prone to flooding as the region gears up for record king tides.
The city is warning that high tides can flood low-lying Bay streets Wednesday morning even without rain.
The highest tides of the year flooded streets, overflowed docks and submerged sidewalks across the Bay Area on Tuesday, prompting concerns about more coastal flooding to come.
High tide reached many Bay Area communities Tuesday morning.
Along San Francisco's Embarcadero, SKY7 footage showed water beginning to overflow barriers and flow onto nearby sidewalks and streets.
Flooding also submerged many locations across Marin County, where officials made last-minute preparations to protect Highway 101 ahead of the peak tides.
Officials said keeping the highway open would be considered a success as tide levels were forecast to reach 8 feet, with the potential to rise as high as 9.5 feet.
They said mitigation efforts performed well during Monday's high tide and expressed confidence in their ability to manage the higher water levels expected Tuesday.
In Sausalito, king tides flooded low-lying areas along Bridgeway and the Marinship district, turning parts of the city into rivers.
The flooding left some drivers navigating through standing water, while others used kayaks and paddle boards in inundated areas. A Coastal Flood Warning remained in effect.
The king tides are coinciding with a fast-moving rainstorm Tuesday night, and wednesday is expected to see even higher tides.
Several major airlines are preemptively bracing for impact ahead of forecasted storms by issuing waivers for some ticketed travelers during the busy Thanksgiving holiday week.
With storms projected from coast to coast and concerns about potential flooding in San Francisco, a number of carriers issued travel waivers for passengers flying in and out of San Francisco on Wednesday.

articles.title_zh: 11 injured in Houthi drone attack on Riyadh tower, Saudi civil defence says
articles.content_orig:
At least 11 people have been wounded following a “terrorist” drone attack by Yemen’s Houthi group on a tower Riyadh’s financial district, according to Saudi authorities and the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
Those injured in Tuesday’s attack include two Saudi citizens, two Indian nationals, three Nepali nationals and four Egyptian nationals, a civil defence spokesperson said.
The Houthi group , which controls much of western Yemen including the capital Sanaa, has been firing at Saudi airports, oil infrastructure and office buildings since Yemen’s ⁠frozen civil war reignited in July in a knock-on from the US-Iran war.
Authorities said emergency services responded immediately and took the necessary measures to protect civilian lives and property.
In a statement, the spokesman of the Saudi-led coalition that supports Yemen’s internationally recognised government against the Houthis said the “cowardly” drone attack targeted the King Abdullah Financial District, adding that authorities are conducting an on-site investigation.
“The deliberate targeting of civilians and civilian objects by the [Houthis] will be met with a firm response,” spokesman Major General Turki al-Maliki said in a post on X.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense posted a picture of the landmark tower housing the headquarters of the Saudi Public Investment Fund, the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund and the country’s tallest skyscraper. The image showed some damage to the building about halfway up the ‌facade.
The Indian Embassy in Saudi Arabia wrote in a post on X it had “learnt that two Indian nationals have sustained injuries in the attack in Riyadh today. The Embassy is ascertaining further details. All possible assistance will be extended to the injured persons and their families.
Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned the “treacherous attack”.
“This attack is a heinous crime and an aggression that reveals the danger of this militia’s terrorist approach and its disregard for innocent lives, which requires a decisive international stance to hold this militia accountable,” AlBudaiwi said in a statement.
He added that the GCC member states stand with the Saudi Arabia and support it in all the measures and actions it takes to safeguard its sovereignty and protect its territory, citizens and residents.
The strike marks the second attack on Riyadh’s financial district in less than a week. An earlier attack on Riyadh caused “material damage”.
The Saudi-led coalition has not named the building that was struck on Tuesday. However, three separate witnesses said a strike targeted the PIF skyscraper.
A fourth witness told the AFP news agency that a vehicle fitted with a speaker had warned pedestrians in the area to take cover.
No warning was sent to phones about any threats to the capital, as has been the case during recent strikes.
Qatar, United Arab Emirates (UAE), Kuwait, Lebanon, the US and Pakistan denounced the attacks on the social media platform X.
UAE said it stood in solidarity with Saudi Arabia “for all measures aimed at safeguarding its security and stability.” Qatar called the attack a “a flagrant violation of Saudi sovereignty”.
Kuwait warned against “the repeated targeting of civilian objects and economic facilities constitutes a dangerous escalation and a direct threat to the lives of civilians.” While Pakistan said the attacks would “heighten regional tensions and and undermine efforts to restore peace and stability.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a call with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud, condemning the “Iran-backed Houthi terrorist attacks on Saudi civilian and energy infrastructure.”
The attacks have caused ⁠the cancellation of most international flights to Riyadh, ⁠and forced Saudi Arabia to postpone or cancel major international events, including soccer’s AFC Asian Cup. On the ground in Yemen, the war has caused a major humanitarian crisis, with ‌hundreds of thousands of people displaced from their homes since July.
The Houthis have seized swathes of territory, forcing forces aligned with the ‌Saudi-backed, ‌internationally recognised government to stage a major retreat this month. The Saudi-led coalition has conducted widespread air strikes.

articles.title_orig: Hostages held in Cartagena, Colombia, supermarket after failed armored car hijacking
articles.title_zh: Hostages held in Cartagena, Colombia, supermarket after failed armored car hijacking
articles.content_orig:
A group of armed men with their faces covered seized a supermarket in the Colombian city of Cartagena on Tuesday and are holding around 25 to 30 hostages, Colombian authorities said.
President Abelardo de la Espriella said that the men were "common criminals" who fled into the supermarket after a failed attempt to hold up an armored truck.
He said in a statement that as of Tuesday evening, five elderly women had been released from the store. Details on the remaining hostages were not given.
The hostage situation broke out as Colombia is experiencing a wave of attacks by rebel groups on government targets, which has recently spread to urban areas.
Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of an Exito supermarket in Cartagena's La Castellana neighborhood, while local media have broadcast images of snipers on nearby buildings in what appears to be a standoff between the armed men and police.
Cartagena is one of Colombia's main tourist destinations. The city of a million people is famous for its well-preserved 18th-century architecture and the thick stone walls built to defend it from pirate attacks.
Cartagena's airport temporarily suspended its operations on Tuesday following the incident. But it later said in a social media post that operations were slowly returning to normal.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s DoJ ‘looked into’ concerns about Huang after affair with suspected Chinese spy but says no security risk found – live
articles.title_zh: Trump’s DoJ ‘looked into’ concerns about Huang after affair with suspected Chinese spy but says no security risk found – live
articles.content_orig:
Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday dodged questions about the conclusions of an investigation President Donald Trump cited to push Nvidia 's board to bring back J ensen Huang as CEO.
Asked by a reporter whether the Department of Justice had investigated Huang and the results of that probe, Blanche said, "What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him."
"And so I'm not going to get into communications I have with the president," Blanche said at a news conference in Washington.
Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday morning, less than two weeks after resigning amid allegations he had affairs with a purported spy for China and two Nvidia employees plus concerns that advanced semiconductor chips made by his company had been diverted to China in violation of U.S. law.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump was asked what led him to personally confirm to Nvidia's board that Huang was not a national security risk.
"We've done a very thorough investigation, and the investigation showed that he did, I mean, he had bad judgment having to do with somewhat unrelated incidents, but he did nothing wrong," Trump replied.
Trump in a Truth Social post on Monday said the U.S. government had no reason to believe Huang's return to the company "poses any risk to National Security," and that Blanche had confirmed the government "does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."
Nvidia, in its statement Monday announcing Huang's return, said, "The Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk."
Blanche on Tuesday said, "Nvidia is a good corporate citizen."
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target, or was the subject of some criminal investigation, or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people," he said.
Patel did not answer a reporter's question of whether the FBI has spoken to Huang and whether the FBI had been made aware of an assessment by U.S. intelligence agencies that Huang's reported paramour, Alice Huang, was an asset for China's spy agency.
Jensen Huang is not related to Alice Huang, who was an executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia's semiconductor chips.
The DOJ and Commerce Department on Nov. 17 said they were investigating Megaspeed for potential diversion of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. export law.
Asked how the DOJ could rule out Jensen Huang having potential criminal liability given the fact that the investigation remains ongoing, Blanche replied, "So, when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about."
"We have hundreds, if not more, export investigations going at any time at the Department of Justice," Blanche said.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Shares Plunge 8% Below IPO Price in Fourth Trading Day
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Shares Plunge 8% Below IPO Price in Fourth Trading Day
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic shares are back trading below the IPO price after a 13% sell-off Tuesday and a 1.5% drop Monday, despite a broad rally in most big tech artificial intelligence names. Trading under $76 on Tuesday, the stock's now 8.5% below its initial public offering level and 34% beneath its intraday high of $115.
It took just four days for ANT to fall under its offering price, compared with 21 trading days for SpaceX , which rallied out of the gate.
Options volume on the stock is picking up as the shares drop and implied volatility jumps to 96, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Almost 500,000 options traded by noon ET on Tuesday for a total premium of about $250 million, the sixth-most active single-stock options in the market, SpotGamma data shows.
Almost 300,000 puts traded versus about 200,000 calls, but the sentiment implied by the trades was not overtly bearish, and judging by the biggest single trades of the day, traders are divided on what happens next.
The biggest single option trade of the day was a $7.5 million purchase of almost 11,000 75-strike puts expiring in mid-December. The trader paid above the ask, suggesting an eagerness to get the trade done at a cost of $6.85, according to SpotGamma. With Anthropic trading at $77, the position needs Anthropic to drop 11% by expiry to pay off.
"Anthropic remains bumpy as investors add risk to other names," said noted tech analyst Dan Ives.
Only one obvious call purchase appeared among the top 10 trades: a 3,000-lot purchase of 85-strike calls expiring Jan. 15 that cost $7.10 each, for a total of $2.2 million. That trade needs Anthropic to rally 19% within the next two months to break even.
Arguably the most interesting action was a string of almost a dozen put sales, ranging from $400,000 to $1.6 million each, all within moments of each other, selling the 120-strike puts expiring Dec. 18. The puts bring in $40 each, meaning the breakeven for the trade is at $80. Selling in-the-money puts in high-volatility stocks is often a way for traders to get long stock without the capital requirements of buying the underlying equity.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say
articles.title_zh: OpenAI Engineer Secretly Recorded Dozens of Meetings, Prosecutors Say
articles.content_orig:
Abdulrahman Alfozan , the Saudi national accused of bugging an OpenAI executive conference room, will be allowed to be released from jail on a $1 million bond , a San Francisco federal court judge ruled Tuesday.
Alfozan, 35, is expected to be released on Wednesday and be fitted with an ankle monitor, according to his attorney, David Rizk.
"We are simply grateful that the Court made the right decision to release Mr. Alfozan and now we look forward to defending the case," Rizk said in a text message after a hearing before U.S. District Court Magistrate Judge Alex Tse.
Tse's ruled in favor of a release motion by Rizk filed last week that said prosecutors had admitted they had "found no new evidence to support the theory that Mr. Alfozan was stealing trade secrets, or to support the speculation that he was acting as an unregistered foreign agent for Saudi Arabia."
The San Francisco U.S. Attorney's Office opposed the former OpenAI engineer's release, saying in its response that he remains a flight risk due to his "considerable resources and ties to Saudi Arabia."
Alfozan's release request "blithely dismisses the seriousness" of the charge he faces, and "appears to presume, without support, that the government's investigation is complete," prosecutors wrote.
Alfozan, who was arrested Oct. 9, is accused of concealing a recording device in the artificial intelligence company's conference room to secretly record discussions. The device was found in a USB port in a television in the room on Sept. 30, prosecutors have said.
Prosecutors said they have found hundreds of audio files on Alfozan's personal computer, "including dozens of recordings of meetings or conversations that occurred at OpenAI throughout September 2026, many of which involve discussions of what may be trade secrets."
Jury selection for Alfozan's trial is scheduled to begin Jan. 20.
Alfozan is a venture partner in a Saudi Arabian venture capital firm that lists Prince Khalid Bin Bader Al Saud , a member of that nation's ruling royal family, as a fellow partner.
OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Alfozan's planned release.
— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela reports $237.5 billion in public debt in step toward massive restructuring
articles.title_zh: Venezuela reports $237.5 billion in public debt in step toward massive restructuring
articles.content_orig:
A cargo ship is loaded at the Bolivarian port of La Guaira, in La Guaira, Venezuela, June 18, 2024. REUTERS/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria
By Mayela Armas, Libby George and Rodrigo Campos
CARACAS/LONDON/NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Venezuela's government put its total debt at $237.5 billion in a long-awaited macroeconomic framework published on Tuesday, providing the clearest picture in years of the country's shattered finances and a potential foundation for one of the world's largest-ever debt restructurings.
In power since 1999, Venezuela's socialist government expects economic output to more than double in the next five years, to $200.9 billion, according to the nearly 200-page document.
The oil-rich country has endured more than a decade of economic crisis marked by widespread shortages of basic necessities, power outages and a migrant crisis that has seen millions of people flee its borders.
Chronic mismanagement and US sanctions imposed on the government of former President Nicolas Maduro also left Venezuela increasingly isolated from the international financial system.
The country defaulted on its international bonds in 2017 and remained largely shut out of global capital markets until US forces seized Maduro during a raid in January, opening the way for renewed international engagement. Maduro is being held in US custody on drug trafficking and other charges.
“We have normalized Venezuela’s representation before multilateral and financial organizations, and we are in advanced discussions to resolve the existing arrears with some of them,” Calixto Ortega, the top economic adviser to acting President Delcy Rodriguez, said on state television on Tuesday.
“We will restructure public debt in a comprehensive manner, and four principles guide us in pursuing this objective: sustainability, comprehensiveness, good faith and transparency.”
The government said in the document, which it posted online, that the country's public debt "is in a state of protracted default and is unsustainable, reflecting the constraints imposed by financial sanctions, the decline in hydrocarbon revenues and years of macroeconomic imbalances."
Although Venezuela's debt pile amounted to 242% of GDP at the end of 2025, the country expects oil production, the key driver of government revenue, to rise by 9.1% a year to 2.9 million barrels per day by 2036.
The framework projects oil export revenue of $30.1 billion this year. It estimates net public hydrocarbon revenue, including state-owned oil company PDVSA's net fiscal position, at $12.8 billion in 2026, rising to $18.4 billion by 2031.
The government also said it planned to adopt a "clear and credible" restructuring plan that would involve all creditor groups.
Such a move could ease concerns among investors that the country might pursue a piecemeal restructuring, which could leave bondholders facing bigger losses.
"We are currently reviewing the information made available by the authorities and it would be premature to comment on specifics at this stage," a spokesperson from the International Monetary Fund said.
"Restoring fiscal and debt sustainability are critical objectives for Venezuela's economic stabilization and recovery. Resuming relations allows Venezuela to exercise its rights and fulfil its obligations as an IMF member, including those related to surveillance, capacity development, and access to IMF financial support, consistent with IMF policies," the spokesperson added.
The Venezuela Creditor Committee, a group representing international bondholders, declined to comment.
The document points to at least $35 billion of PDVSA's nonfinancial obligations, as well as part of a $240 million BANDES bank loan, as "intra-public-sector" debt, meaning the headline $237.5 billion in debt is not only owed to external creditors.
The document does not specify how those types of claims would be treated in an eventual restructuring.
Centerview, the financial advisory firm managing Venezuela's restructuring process, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
After the government report, Venezuela's sovereign bonds, as well as those issued by PDVSA, rose between 2.25 and 6.4 cents on the dollar.
The country's eurobond debt totaled $110.1 billion, including $45.9 billion of past-due interest, according to the report. Its debt to China, part of what it owes in bilateral loans, is $16.68 billion, while it owes Russia $5.08 billion, the document showed.
Venezuela announced plans to restructure its debt in May and promised to release key numbers within a month. However, devastating twin earthquakes in June, which rocked the northwestern and central parts of the country and killed at least 6,500 people, further complicated efforts to assess the state of the economy.
Since the seizure of Maduro, Rodriguez, also a socialist, has made attracting international investment a core priority — particularly in the long-neglected but crucial oil and gas sector.
Oil production fell from 2.8 million barrels per day in 2012 to just over 1 million bpd last year.
The country has secured investment pledges from private companies and hosted a string of investor trips, while also overhauling its oil laws to attract capital.
But attracting investment on the scale Venezuela needs will be difficult without resolving its defaulted debt. The government, in its macroeconomic framework, said it was committed to doing so.
"The scale, diversity and legal complexity of these obligations underscore the need for a comprehensive approach to public debt normalization," it said, adding: "Restoring public debt sustainability will require a comprehensive approach anchored in a credible macroeconomic stabilization program and supported by strengthened institutional frameworks."
The country's economy will grow 5% this year, the document said. Inflation is set to rise but will slow in the medium term to an average of 24%.
While the macroeconomic framework provides a clearer picture of the country's finances, investors are still awaiting a comprehensive debt sustainability analysis that will help determine how much Venezuela can afford to repay, based on expected financial flows, reserve accumulation and total debt-servicing costs.
The Venezuelan communications ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on when that analysis would be published.
(Reporting by Libby George, Mayela Armas and Rodrigo Campos; additional reporting by Marc Jones; editing by Karin Strohecker, Paul Simao and Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title_orig: Thanksgiving dinner prices hit an all-time high – and one staple is driving the surge
articles.title_zh: Thanksgiving dinner prices hit an all-time high – and one staple is driving the surge
articles.content_orig:
Lydia Hu reports from Hamilton, New Jersey, on how turkey farmers like Artie DiPaola are raising prices this holiday season due to rising production costs.
Americans are facing higher costs this holiday season amid stubborn inflation and the cost of Thanksgiving festivities has increased from last year, a new analysis finds.
The American Institute for Economic Research (AIER) compiled its 2026 Thanksgiving Cost Index, which showed that prices rose 2.6% over the last year to reach an all-time high.
Prices are now significantly higher than they were before the COVID-19 pandemic, with the Thanksgiving Cost Index now up 32.1% from its 2019 level, as the post-pandemic inflation surge never receded even as the pace of price increases slowed.
"Inflation has moderated considerably since 2021 and 2022, but the cumulative increases in food prices are still a substantial burden on American households," AIER senior director of research Peter C. Earle told FOX Business.
THANKSGIVING TRAVEL TO DIP FOR FIRST TIME IN YEARS AS HIGHER COSTS WEIGH ON AMERICANS
Turkey and poultry prices rose at more than double the rate of other components in AIER's Thanksgiving Cost Index, Earle said. (Liz Clayman/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Earle noted that prices for turkey and other poultry jumped 8.4% over the past year, which was more than double the price increase for any other component of AIER's Thanksgiving Cost Index – which will be a notable jump given that turkey is the centerpiece of many Americans' Thanksgiving dinners.
"Renewed avian influenza outbreaks, higher diesel costs, and the unusually concentrated seasonal demand for turkeys have pushed prices sharply higher despite an increase in domestic production," Earle said.
THANKSGIVING SHOPPERS FACE HIGHER TURKEY PRICES AS FAMILY FARMS STRUGGLE WITH RISING COSTS
Thanksgiving food prices rose 2.6% from a year ago in AIER's analysis. (Robert Nickelsberg/Getty Images)
Thanksgiving food prices overall were up 2.6% in the past year, whereas the cost of meals at home was up 1.8% and food consumed away from home was up 3.5%.
Bread prices have risen 3.3% in the last year, while prices for frozen vegetables were up 2.6%, and canned fruits like cranberry sauce rose 2.3%.
"Those differences make clear that inflation can vary considerably across narrow categories of consumer spending ," Earle said.
FED'S PREFERRED INFLATION GAUGE ROSE IN SEPTEMBER AS THIRD-QUARTER GDP BEATS EXPECTATIONS
Thanksgiving costs are 32.1% higher than they were in 2019 before the pandemic-era inflation surge, AIER noted. (John Moore/Getty Images)
Earle also emphasized the significance of post-pandemic inflation by noting that AIER's Thanksgiving Cost Index surged nearly 17.5% in a single year between September 2021 and September 2022.
"That extraordinary increase remains embedded in today's prices," he said.
"Slower inflation doesn't reverse previous price increases, which is why so many Americans continue to experience financial pressure – even as headline inflation has receded," Earle added.

articles.title_orig: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
articles.title_zh: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
articles.content_orig:
Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.
It’s too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.
The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There’s not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, “It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field.”
The proof of the hypothesis was announced by a mathematician named Levent Alpöge, who has been working at Anthropic, and, not surprisingly, used Claude to generate it. His announcement is written in a somewhat florid style (example: “one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph”), and he has apparently dropped some hints that some of it was meant in jest.
But it does make clear that this proof was a longstanding interest of Alpöge’s, and he had some insights into how to connect different areas of math to reach the final proof. The process seems to have involved getting the AI started with handling a simplified “toy” form of some of Alpöge’s insights and then directing it to expand what it found there to the full scope of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof itself comes in two different forms, and the difference between them gets at the heart of why AI usage in math has been controversial. One is a rigorous description of the proof using a programming language named Lean that has allowed the rapid verification that the proof is valid. The second is a description of the logic behind it, which may ultimately be the key for mathematics as a field to benefit from this proof.
It’s important to emphasize that, so far at least, AI has been solving problems that humans previously recognized as significant. That significance is typically ascribed to mathematical ideas because of their implications or utility—they either tell us something about areas of math that people care about, or they keep popping up in problems that mathematicians are working on. So far, there are no indications that AI can recognize or formulate interesting and important unresolved problems on its own.
But AI has tackled many problems humans have considered significant with impressive ease. Trained on a body of material that included a lot of advanced math, the software has provided both formal proofs as well as counterexamples that have clearly demonstrated that some proposals are incorrect.
When it comes to proofs, AI might have some advantages over people. For starters, it’s not specialized in specific fields of math and can potentially pull together tools from a variety of disciplines. AI also pays no cost (either in terms of career or emotional soundness) from going down the wrong track, giving up, and starting over.
AI models have also had one of their biggest limitations removed via humanity’s development of Lean, a computer language that allows mathematical proofs to be expressed in a way that can be readily verified. Due to their tendency to hallucinate, a description of a proof generated by an AI would still require extensive human validation before it could be accepted, a task that might radically shift the effort/reward ratio of using AI models. But by instructing an AI to include the necessary Lean code as part of its output, verification has become straightforward.
The unfortunate aspect of this for mathematics as a field is that it’s often the process of working through the reasoning behind a proof, rather than the step-by-step logic, that advances the field as a whole.
Mathematicians have expressed their fears about this aspect of AI usage in a formal open letter . We’ll try to connect those fears to the recent announcement.
Before AI, proofs were typically worked through by people who recognized potential pathways connecting disparate fields of math and spent years finding ways to formalize those intuitions and validate that the math worked. It wasn’t necessarily an efficient use of time if the only output was the proof itself.
But that was rarely the case. By finding the connections between problems, this work helped many other people see new ways of tackling whatever issues they were wrestling with. Mathematicians often developed new tools, found shortcuts, or stumbled across related problems while working through their proofs, enriching math as a whole. In other words, the proof itself was often less important for math than the process of generating it.
By contrast, the internal workings of large neural networks are notoriously opaque. Asking an AI to explain its reasoning runs into the same problems that asking it anything else does: Since the software has only been selected for producing decent-sounding text, it’s likely to make something up that sounds good when asked about its own internal processes. So, an AI-generated proof has little to offer the field in terms of new ideas or unexpected advances, at least on its own.
Indeed, nobody can say much about the Riemann proof at the moment, simply because mathematicians have barely started the process of shifting through the logic as expressed in Lean. It’s possible it can eventually produce new insights and tools, but it may take years before humans can figure out what they are and how to express them in a way that other mathematicians can appreciate.
How mathematicians are expected to identify new challenges that can push their fields beyond the current body while seeing AI relieve them of the need to actually do math is anybody’s guess.
This is all new and progressing incredibly quickly; there has been no time for the field to find a new normal. It’s possible that, once Alpöge gets around to describing the approach he pushed Claude to use, mathematicians will start getting the same sorts of insights that they normally expect to receive from proofs. It could be that Alpöge’s approach, mixing human intuition with machine-generated detail and rigor, provides a model for what math will look like in a few years.
But it’s impossible to tell at this early stage in development.

articles.title_orig: Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends
articles.title_zh: Reform bid to oust presiding officer fails after its Senedd boycott ends
articles.content_orig:
An attempt by Reform UK to remove the Senedd's Presiding Officer has failed, following a passionate speech to the Welsh Parliament by Huw Irranca-Davies.
Members of the Senedd (MSs) rejected Reform's motion by 55 votes to 29.
Earlier the party ended a two-week boycott of most proceedings in the chamber after one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration.
Irranca-Davies, whose title is Llywydd, said his duty was to "apply the rules fairly and impartially".
Reform's Llyr Powell said: "If you had a problem with what Joe Martin said, debate him, don't shut him down."
A source close to Irranca-Davies had "wholly refuted" Reform's accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber.
Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".
Responding to Reform's attempt to remove him on Tuesday evening, the presiding office gave a long and passionate speech in defence of his role, which prompted a standing ovation from the other Cardiff Bay parties.
"The duty of the chair is not to please, it is not to flatter, not to avoid controversy, it is to apply the rules fairly and impartially, irrespective of pressure, of popularity or of political consequence," he said.
"Parliamentary privilege has never meant that anything goes, it has never meant speech without standards, it has never meant rights without responsibilities.
"Without rules, eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard. "Without rules intimidation begins to replace persuasion, without rules scrutiny deteriorates into shouting."
After losing the vote, which Reform had no realistic prospect of winning, its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said it was "now clear that the establishment parties are content to see a Member of this Senedd silenced".
"We will continue to fight for the rights of elected members to represent their constituents as they see fit," she said.
At the start of the afternoon session, without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon . Martin was not among them.
Jenner began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us?"
"It's been a little bit duller without us in here," she added.
In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram".
Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November.
The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech.
The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised.
Shortly after its members had returned to the Senedd chamber, the party sent journalists a statement from Jenner.
She said the party "thought we were approaching a sensible resolution" in talks with the Llywydd that would allow Martin "to return to the chamber without apologising for the speech he made in the Senedd".
"It has become clear this morning that the Llywydd has not been negotiating in good faith and has changed his mind at the eleventh hour," Jenner said.
"He has admitted to us that his decisions on this matter have been influenced by the feelings of outside organisations.
"It is now for him to explain to the people of Wales which organisations they are and what that means for Welsh democracy.
"We now have no choice but to escalate this situation."
The Senedd's authorities strongly denied Reform's "completely inaccurate" claims and said the Llywydd's position had remained the same since he ruled against Martin.
A source close to Irranca-Davies said he was "always clear" during four meetings with Reform that Martin needed to apologise.
Irranca-Davies, who chairs Senedd plenary sessions, left the chamber during First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon.
A spokesperson for the Llywydd said he met Jenner "entirely in good faith and had hoped to continue these confidential discussions constructively".
"It is unfortunate that they have chosen this course of action," the spokesperson added.
"While the Llywydd is disappointed, he respects the democratic process.
"Just as members elected him to this role, it is right that they have the opportunity to decide whether he continue to have their confidence."

articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow up 350 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq decline a day after Nvidia's 31% surge; Dell results on tap: live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow up 350 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq decline a day after Nvidia's 31% surge; Dell results on tap: live updates
articles.content_orig:
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures are sliding on Tuesday morning, November 24, 2026, as Wall Street cools off from Monday’s blistering tech rally and shifts its focus back to Federal Reserve rate-hike risks, fresh Iran sanctions, and crucial inflation data due before the Thanksgiving holiday.
Early premarket trading shows losses concentrated heavily in technology and artificial intelligence shares , while the blue-chip Dow is experiencing a more modest pullback ahead of the 9:30 a.m. ET opening bell.
As of roughly 7:04 to 7:33 a.m. ET, all three major U.S. equity index futures were trading in the red:
Tuesday’s dip is largely a breather after one of Wall Street’s most explosive sessions in years. On Monday, November 23, the Dow surged 3.01%, the S&P 500 jumped 4.73%, and the Nasdaq Composite soared 6.51% —marking the biggest single-day gains for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 2025.
That rally was triggered by Nvidia’s stunning decision to reinstate co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO , which sent Nvidia shares skyrocketing 31.5% —its best day in 23 years—and restored nearly $1 trillion in market value. Still, a nalysts say Huang’s return does not erase deeper investor jitters over debt-funded AI data center spending , regulatory scrutiny, or Huang’s upcoming congressional testimony on December 3.
"Nvidia’s stock price decline on Tuesday is to be expected after such a large rally in the previous session," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. "The return of Huang does not mean that the challenges facing AI are over."
Beyond tech profit-taking, macroeconomic and geopolitical headwinds are pressuring futures. Traders are now pricing in a 95% probability of a 25-basis-point interest rate hike at the Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting—along with a 5% chance of a jumbo 50-basis-point increase, according to CME Group’s FedWatch tool. New York Fed President John Williams reinforced those concerns Monday, stating that persistently high inflation points toward tighter monetary policy.
The rapid whipsaw in AI stocks is also testing Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh, with Evercore ISI’s Krishna Guha warning that talk of faster tightening adds stress while Warsh’s silence leaves markets guessing on his stance. The rate-sensitive 2-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.67%.
Geopolitical tensions added another layer of caution after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced new U.S. sanctions targeting Iranian exchange houses, front companies, and key personnel, alongside reports of tanker incidents east of the Strait of Hormuz. Even so, energy and metals traded lower early Tuesday, with Brent crude dipping to $88.75 a barrel (near a three-month low), gold easing to $3,619.70 an ounce, and copper giving back 3%.
While steep red numbers in premarket trading can look alarming, strategists emphasize that Tuesday’s pullback is not a market crash—and gives back only a fraction of Monday’s massive gains. Even a 1.5% to 2% dip in Nasdaq futures barely dents the index’s 6.5% surge from the prior session.
Overseas markets also reflected lingering momentum from Monday’s U.S. rebound: Taiwanese shares rallied 9% (with TSMC and Foxconn nearing their 10% daily limits), South Korea’s Kospi jumped roughly 6.3% to 7%, and Japan’s Nikkei climbed nearly 4%, while Europe’s STOXX 600 slipped just 0.1%. Because premarket futures trade on thinner volume overnight, early losses can still narrow—or reverse—once regular U.S. trading begins at 9:30 a.m. ET.

articles.title_orig: Iraqi PM cracks down on Kurds' control of oilfields, Kurds reject risky move
articles.title_zh: Iraqi PM cracks down on Kurds' control of oilfields, Kurds reject risky move
articles.content_orig:
Iraq’s Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has ordered the federal Ministry of Oil to manage oilfields in areas under Kurdish security control, potentially deepening tensions between Baghdad and the semi-autonomous region in the north of the country.
The prime minister’s order covers oilfields in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces, according to a statement from his office on Tuesday.
It said Baghdad would “secure and monitor all oilfields with cameras, including fields within the administrative boundaries of the federal government that are under the security authority of the regional government”.
Al-Zaidi also ordered the border crossings authority to take over all crossings in the Kurdish region and directed the regional government to approve exports of crude oil and petroleum products only through the federal Oil Ministry.
“The Border Forces Command shall close unofficial crossings along the international borders with neighbouring countries, including crossings in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq,” the statement said, adding that “all seasonal roads” between the four governorates and the Kurdish region would be closed.
Masoud Barzani, the president of the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the former president of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, called the decision “troubling”.
In his view, it was another attempt at undermining “the principles of federalism and the Iraqi constitution, disregard the rights of the people of Kurdistan, and advance reckless and ill-considered proposals”, according to a statement citing him by the KDP foreign relations office.
“From the outset, we expressed our support for Prime Minister Ali Zaidi and his efforts to resolve outstanding problems. We have also supported the fight against corruption and taken practical steps toward that end,” Barzani said.
“Yet the region now faces a misleading and unjust campaign, with unfounded accusations published against it daily.”
The KDP leader said that his party is ready to cooperate with the government in preventing illegal activities and smuggling, “but this must be done through legal and constitutional channels”.
Al Jazeera’s Mahmoud Abdelwahed, reporting from Baghdad, said the latest development might exacerbate tensions and disputes over control of oil and the sharing of budgetary resources between the national government and the autonomous regional government.
“The federal government is keen to keep all excavation and marketing of oil under its state organisation, SOMO, but this has been totally rejected by the Kurdish region,” he said.
A dispute over Kurdish authorities selling oil without Baghdad’s approval halted pipeline shipments to Turkiye for more than two years before the sides agreed in September 2025 to restart them.
Al-Zaidi, meanwhile, removed the head of the border crossings authority and suspended North Oil Company’s director general and his deputies pending further investigation, Iraq’s state news agency reported.
In a separate case, Iraqi officials accused Kataib Hezbollah, an armed group backed by Iran, of running an oil smuggling network in its stronghold of Jurf al-Sakhar, south of Baghdad.
The group denied the accusation.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian Drones Hit 22 Russian Vehicles, Including 14 Tanks, in Zaporizhzhia Raid
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian Drones Hit 22 Russian Vehicles, Including 14 Tanks, in Zaporizhzhia Raid
articles.content_orig:
Special forces from the National Guard of Ukraine’s Lasar’s Group struck 22 pieces of Russian military equipment in the Zaporizhzhia region during a single special operation, including 14 tanks.
The overnight operation resulted in the destruction of two tanks and one truck, while 12 tanks, two command and staff vehicles, two pieces of engineering equipment, and three trucks were damaged, according to Lasar’s Group on Facebook on November 24.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Analysts first gathered intelligence on the area where the Russian equipment was concentrated, and then aerial reconnaissance followed. Recon drone teams from Lasar’s Group provided exact details on where the Russian gear sat deep behind the line of contact in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Strike drones from the unit were then sent deep into territory held by Russia during the overnight operation. The unit reported that the strike took place last night and hit a mix of armored and support vehicles.
“Since 2022, the key task of the ‘Group of Lazar’ special unit of the National Guard of Ukraine has been the destruction of Russian military equipment. This applies, in particular, to tanks, which created huge problems for the infantry. In almost five years, we have destroyed more than 2,400 tanks and continue to successfully hunt them, as we did during our recent special operation,” Lasar’s Group wrote on Facebook.
“The entire special operation was carried out by Lazar’s Group, and the total damage inflicted on the enemy reaches tens of millions of dollars. Russians must remember: no matter how many tanks they produce, we will burn them all,” Lasar’s Group added.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian special forces struck two Russian brigade-level ammunition depots near temporarily occupied Oleshky in Kherson region after detecting Russian military activity during a humanitarian ceasefire intended to facilitate civilian evacuations.
The strikes were conducted by the Separate Diving Detachment of the Omega Special Forces Center of Ukraine’s National Guard, which released footage of the operation on November 12.

articles.title_orig: Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
articles.title_zh: Trump wanted Jensen Huang back. Now, the president is all alone in Washington
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump wanted Jensen Huang back at the helm of Nvidia . Now that the chip mogul is reinstated, Trump is cheering alone in Washington.
Trump celebrated and claimed credit after Huang was reinstated by the Nvidia board on Monday, a stunning return to power for the embattled CEO. In a nearly hourlong phone call with CNBC , the president went as far as saying he "made the deal" to bring Huang back.
But Trump's jubilation stands in stark contrast to the reaction from even his staunchest allies on Capitol Hill , who recoiled after the reinstatement and vowed to continue their investigations into Huang — whose relationship with a potential Chinese intelligence asset they fear may have jeopardized U.S. national security.
"The risk remains that there could be information that a Chinese spy knows about a key individual in the supply chain, and that's not worth the risk," Sen. Kevin Cramer , R-N.D., said Tuesday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang for crying out loud ... just to make sure that he doesn't do something that's going to risk the United States."
Trump's rare isolation from his party over Huang comes after the GOP was throttled in the midterm elections , as Democrats rode a blue tsunami to capture the Senate and the largest House majority this century. And it suggests Republicans, who have spent a decade in lockstep with the president, may have found an issue on which they can't bring themselves to take Trump's side.
"I can accept what the president has done," Cramer said. "But we have to put guardrails around to protect the United States of America."
Many midterm voters identified Silicon Valley's most visible outputs, artificial intelligence and data centers, as top concerns motivating them to cast ballots for Democrats. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey in October found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while just 13% support one.
By timing his extraordinary intervention in Nvidia so soon after the GOP's historic losses, Trump could spark a national debate about corporate governance and responsibility, former Under Secretary of State Richard Stengel said.
"With the repudiation of Trumpism in the midterms and voter revulsion with corruption, I think there will be a turn back to a more value-based duty of care for boards of directors and away from the current maximization of shareholder value," Stengel told CNBC in an email.
"Directors are citizens first, shareholders second. The idea that you put profit above national security should disgust shareholders, not please them," Stengel, who worked in the Obama administration, wrote.
Bipartisan lawmakers are now racing to pass a series of export control bills before the year ends, a call that has only grown louder since Huang was reinstated.
There's "not just frustration or political worry, but actual, substantive national security concern here from Democrats and Republicans," Chris McGuire, senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told CNBC.
"This has historically been a bipartisan issue," McGuire said. "Democrats and Republicans generally pretty much agree that we shouldn't be sending our most advanced chips to China."
"If it happened in massive quantities, people want to know why, how, and they want to make sure that it doesn't happen again," he said. "And putting your thumb on the scale in this clear of a way seems like it could undercut those efforts."
The White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the political dynamics of Trump's involvement in reinstating Huang.
Republicans will have the first crack at investigating Huang next week before ceding power to Democrats in January. Democrats have vowed their own investigations into the Nvidia CEO and his ties to the president and his Cabinet. The Democrats who will lead those investigations are now hopeful that Republicans will join them.
"I've been seeing a lot of Republicans outraged and scandalized by what has just happened," House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin , D-Md., said Tuesday on "Squawk Box," when asked if Republicans may support a bipartisan investigation of Nvidia.
"When else in American history can you think of a time when a president of the United States called up a corporate board of directors meeting and then essentially dictated to them who was going to be their new CEO right after they had fired the guy?"
Trump throughout his second term has stated repeatedly that achieving AI dominance is required for the U.S. to maintain global superiority. His administration has championed the rapid growth of the country's tech giants and forged close ties with its leaders, especially Huang, while removing constraints on the industry and opposing some new regulatory efforts.
At the same time, Trump has defended Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick against accusations of slow-walking export controls on China, the fiercest competitor in the AI race. And while Trump recently discussed AI during an in-person meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, he appeared to deliver few demands and achieved few assurances about Beijing's efforts to acquire U.S. chips.
"To say we can't do AI safety because of China, and then also be actively loosening the controls on China, makes no sense," McGuire said.
Some of Trump's fiercest allies have raised similar qualms.
"Reinstating Jensen Huang is going to blow back on our national security,"  MAGA activist Laura Loomer wrote in an X post Monday. "Eventually there has to be accountability for jeopardizing US national security. China didn't just get access to Nvidia chips by accident."
Newt Gingrich, the influential former Republican speaker of the House, in an X post after Huang's reinstatement, wrote, "Congress should really dig into this as a national security issue of enormous proportions and also a significant failure in the federal bureaucracy."
Their criticisms sharply contrast with the praise coming from Silicon Valley and some of the Trump-friendly voices within it, such as Elon Musk , who wrote Monday, "The mistake has been corrected."
But that's a shrinking political constituency, McGuire said.
"The tech-right perspective is very out of touch with where most of the Republican Party is on these issues, to say nothing of the Democratic Party," he said.
"Those positions are just not going to be sustainable for much longer," he added. "I think they're already becoming unsustainable."
