Micron Technology (MU) shares tracked lower in morning trade on Tuesday after BNP Paribas downgraded the memory-chip maker and cut its price target by more than half, warning that demand risks could emerge in 2028 even as the AI boom drives memory sales.
In a note to investors cited by TheFly, BNP Paribas analyst Karl Ackerman lowered his rating to ‘Neutral’ from ‘Outperform’ and cut his price target to $775 from $1,700. The new target is roughly 54% below his previous estimate, but still implies about 9.5% upside from Monday's close of $707.70.
MU stock fell over 7% in morning trade amid broader market weakness. Shares had surged 19% on Monday, their biggest one-day gain in six months, amid a broader market rebound following Nvidia's (NVDA) reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang .
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Ackerman said risks are building around hyperscalers' capacity plans for 2028, which could threaten the memory industry's supply-demand balance. BNP also pointed to a reduction in high-bandwidth memory (HBM) content in Nvidia's Vera Rubin Ultra platform.
The analyst also expects PC and mobile unit sales to decline in 2026 and 2027, while additional wafer capacity comes online.
More production capacity could increase chip supply at a time when demand growth may be slowing, putting pressure on memory pricing.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
BNP's cautious outlook contrasts with Micron's expectations for continued supply constraints.
In its latest earnings call, Micron said it expects demand to outstrip supply in both 2027 and 2028, and that it still has no clear timeline for when the market will return to balance. The company also said it had secured commitments for the vast majority of its 2027 high-bandwidth memory supply.
Reports about Nvidia adjusting memory specifications for its next-generation AI systems surfaced earlier this year. TrendForce reported in October that Samsung and SK Hynix (SKHY) were preparing lower-spec 8-Hi HBM4 memory for the platform, with production expected in 2027. The reports also suggested Nvidia was reducing memory bandwidth requirements, potentially easing supply constraints.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Nvidia has not publicly confirmed the reported changes, and the reports did not identify Micron as directly affected.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around Micron trended in ‘bullish’ territory over the past day, accompanied by chatter at ‘high’ levels.
Micron shares have fallen over 40% from their June peak. BNP’s $775 price target is also far below the roughly $1,593 average target from analysts tracked by Koyfin. Data showed 28 ‘Buy’ ratings, two ‘Hold’ ratings and no ‘Sell’ ratings among 30 analysts covering the stock.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Micron shares are still up roughly 241% over the past year, despite the correction from June highs.

articles.title_orig: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.title_zh: US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation
articles.content_orig:
When Jensen Huang was shockingly reinstalled as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, both Nvidia’s board of directors and President Donald Trump cast it as the result of the administration’s assurances that he wasn’t a national security risk and faced no legal jeopardy.
But pretty much ever since then, those assurances have appeared less than ironclad.
All of which reinforces what a massive risk both Trump and Nvidia just took , which should be ratcheting up concerns among some very skeptical GOP lawmakers .
The board said in its initial statement Monday morning that its talks with senior government officials left it “confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk” — despite the fact that he had an affair with a woman who US officials feared could be working with Chinese intelligence.
Trump said shortly thereafter on social media that the US government “has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
Trump also said that, despite questions about prohibited Nvidia chips making their way to China, Attorney General Todd Blanche “has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct.”
But other officials have yet to publicly double down on those assurances. And Blanche was rather evasive in an interview Monday night. Even Trump has repeatedly emphasized very real caveats.
In addition to the assurances he offered on Truth Social on Monday morning, Trump in a later CNBC interview claimed the Justice Department had “exonerated” Huang .
“They did a study. They did a pretty good investigation,” Trump said. “And they felt that he himself was exonerated. I don’t know what word you want to use.”
The US Commerce and Justice Departments previously said investigators had conducted an in-person interview with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as part of an investigation into whether the Singaporean-based company had been diverting US semiconductors.
But now Blanche is talking around all that, with increasingly evasive comments about what sort of investigations have occurred or been opened — even accusing reporters of “mocking” him by asking the questions.
“What I said last week is that we were looking into it,” Blanche said at the Justice Department on Tuesday. “The FBI, law enforcement, looks into things all the time. That doesn’t necessarily become a criminal investigation. Doesn’t necessarily become an indictment. It just literally is that it’s looking into things.”
Pressed on whether Jensen Huang had been investigated, Blanche threw the question back at reporters. “What does that mean, had Huang been investigated? For what?”
He went on to say, “I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.”
And the night before, when Fox News host Laura Ingraham asked whether Huang had been cleared of being a national security risk and of illegal activity, Blanche never offered a direct answer.
He instead referred to a Wall Street Journal story Ingraham had mentioned in her lead-up, and declined to comment on it. Then he mentioned extensive discussions within the administration — but without ever saying that those discussions had confirmed Huang was in the clear.
Blanche eventually landed on saying: “A lot of thoughtful process by administration officials went into this decision, and the right decision was reached, I believe.”
And perhaps most strikingly, despite Trump’s claim that the DOJ had “exonerated” Huang, Blanche wouldn’t even confirm the DOJ had opened an investigation.
Ingraham asked twice whether the investigation was now closed, and Blanche balked.
“That assumes there’s an investigation that’s open. And I — that’s never been discussed publicly,” Blanche said.
That’s a long way from Trump’s claim about Huang having been “exonerated.”
While Blanche was evasive, others in the administration were non-existent when it came to vouching for Trump’s assurances.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio was a case in point.
It was Rubio who disseminated a memo to senior US officials warning about potential counterintelligence risks posed by Huang’s affair with Alice Huang (no relation).
But on Monday, Rubio said nothing publicly about Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.
He ignored a CNN reporter’s shouted question about it during a public event with a foreign dignitary.
Maybe that wasn’t the forum for an in-depth answer on the subject. But Rubio would seem to be a hugely significantly witness for Trump’s assurances. And the fact that the administration didn’t put him forward was conspicuous.
And even Trump, later Monday morning in his CNBC interview, qualified his assurances.
When talking about whether Huang might have known about prohibited chips making their way to China, Trump said that “he certainly did not know about it.”
But then he quickly added a less-than-certain caveat, appending “or at least that’s been our very powerful impression.”
Later in the interview, Trump twice qualified his assurances about Huang’s lack of legal liability by saying that “we believe” Huang is in the clear.
“I gave them enough assurance,” Trump added.
He later said: “You can only give the assurance as to what you know. But we feel very strongly that he’s in good shape — very good shape.”
None of these comments preclude something else coming out about Huang.
Perhaps Trump and those around him are indeed very confident that nothing is going to come out to undercut their assurances. But they just won’t completely own those assurances yet.
And Blanche’s evasive interview and Rubio’s lack of comment both suggest this could be a familiar dynamic: Trump coming to a conclusion based upon what he wants to believe, and those around him scrambling to justify and bolster his preferred narrative.
But there seem to be plenty of people bent on learning more. And time will tell how well the administration’s qualified assurances hold up.

articles.title_orig: Top Denmark court upholds law allowing eviction of "non-Western" residents from "ghettos"
articles.title_zh: Top Denmark court upholds law allowing eviction of "non-Western" residents from "ghettos"
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court upheld on Monday a controversial law intended to eliminate ethnic enclaves in public housing, or "ghettos," as the government calls them, by giving authorities the ability to limit the number of "non-Western" immigrants and their descendants who can live in any particular housing development.
The court ruled that the eviction in 2022 of residents from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej, a housing development in the city of Helsingør, north of Copenhagen, did not constitute ethnic discrimination.
The Danish law introduced in 2018 is among Europe's most aggressive attempts to force immigrant communities to assimilate and to avoid the evolution of "parallel societies" in the country. It has attracted both international condemnation and admiration from politicians in other countries that seek to emulate Denmark's approach to immigration and integration.
Under the legislation, residential areas with at least 1,000 inhabitants, where more than 50% of residents are immigrants or descendants of immigrants from "non-Western" countries, and which meet certain socioeconomic criteria relating to employment rates, income levels, education attainment, and crime, can be subject to redevelopment requirements.
Housing developments designated as "transformation areas" are required to reduce the proportion of public family housing to no more than 40% by 2030. This can involve demolishing buildings, selling properties to private landlords, or converting them to other forms of housing, resulting in the eviction and relocation of some residents.
Under the law, non-Western countries include all nations outside the European Union, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Vatican State, the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand. The classification is based on a person's country of origin rather than their citizenship, which means even Danish citizens born and raised in Denmark can be classified as non-Western if both of their parents immigrated from non-Western countries.
The seven families evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej argued in their case that the distinction between Western and non-Western origins was effectively a proxy for ethnicity, and thus amounts to illegal discrimination based on race. The Supreme Court concluded that the distinction was based on nationality and country of birth rather than ethnicity, however, noting that both categories encompassed a wide range of ethnic groups and that people of the same ethnicity could fall into either category.
The court's ruling followed a decision last December by the European Union's highest court, which found that the Danish legislation could constitute discrimination on the grounds of ethnic origin, but the EU court left it to Denmark's courts to make the final determination.
Anders Svendsen, Chief Legal Officer for Denmark's national tenants' organization, LLO, told CBS News the organization didn't expect the Supreme Court to rule the way it did.
"We were slightly surprised, considering what the EU court had come up with previously last December," he said.
The organization estimates that several thousand homes have been demolished under the legislation already.
"A lot of people are still quite concerned, because they don't know if they're going to be next," Svendsen said. "This regulation has been quite unpopular among the renters in the public sector, but it has been quite popular in the population at large."
The LLO said it recognized the government's desire to promote social cohesion, but it questioned whether demolishing homes and reducing the availability of affordable housing was a proportionate response.
"We disagree, because it sees public housing as a problem to be solved and less public housing is seen as the cure," Svendsen told CBS News.
Joachim B. Olsen, a former Danish lawmaker who is now the opinion editor for the Danish newspaper B.T., was not surprised by Monday's ruling.
"Legislation is thoroughly vetted by the Department of Justice to make sure that it is in accordance with the constitution and Denmark's international obligations before it is presented to parliament," he told CBS News.
Olsen rejected the suggestion that the distinction between Western and non-Western origin was a proxy for race, arguing that it was based on cultural background.
"It is important to understand that the provisions in the 'ghetto law' apply to anyone living in the area designated as a 'ghetto,' no matter ethnicity or citizenship," he said.
Olsen argued that the policy had been broadly successful. According to Danish government figures , the number of neighborhoods officially classified as ghettos fell from 29 in 2018, to five in 2025.
"Incomes in these areas have risen. Employment is up. So is the educational level," he said. "Overall, I would say that positives outnumber the negatives."
Denmark has become a model for some other European governments as they look at ways to tighten immigration restrictions and address public concerns over the integration of immigrant communities.
While demands for tougher immigration policy in many European nations have been driven predominantly by right-wing populist parties, Denmark's restrictive approach has been championed by its center-left Social Democratic Party, led by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Frederiksen has been outspoken about her desire to preserve Danish culture and her opposition to a concept of multiculturalism in which all cultures are afforded equal standing in the country.
"We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe," Frederiksen said last week on the B.T. newspaper's podcast, Borgerlig Tabloid . "Of course, this evolves when new people arrive here. But it is also necessary that, in the future, Denmark still has a strong majority culture."
Britain's government cited Denmark's policies earlier this year as it changed its own rules on people granted asylum in the U.K.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, announcing a new policy in March under which people granted asylum will have that status subject to regular review, said the "reset in Britain's asylum offer" had been "inspired by Denmark's success."
Denmark has also been at the forefront of efforts to establish "return hubs" — deportation centers outside Europe.
Last week, Denmark joined Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands in announcing plans to establish a "return hub" in Rwanda for migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in Europe, but who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.

articles.title_orig: US preparing to raise tariffs on China, EU and a dozen other countries
articles.title_zh: US preparing to raise tariffs on China, EU and a dozen other countries
articles.content_orig:
The United States is finalizing a new round of tariffs against China, the EU, and a dozen other countries accused by the Department of Commerce of harming U.S. industry by subsidizing their domestic manufacturers, according to The Wall Street Journal . This is the latest move by the Trump administration to fully restore the trade wall that the president erected on April 2 of last year with indiscriminate tariffs on the entire world, but which were overturned by the Supreme Court.
Several U.S. media outlets are expecting U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer to announce the results of the tariff investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 this week. The Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) has been analyzing for several months whether 16 jurisdictions have policies that favor surplus production, a practice that drives down prices and harms the U.S. industry. Greer’s team is investigating alleged industrial aid from China, the European Union, and 14 other countries.
The investigation began last March, after the Supreme Court’s setback . The court overturned the indiscriminate trade levies because it considered that Trump had exceeded his authority by invoking the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) to approve tariffs, when this law did not authorize him to do so.
After that reversal, the USTR opened two investigations based on Article 301: one directed at 60 jurisdictions (about a hundred countries) for violating export regulations on forced labor; and the other against 16 jurisdictions for promoting surplus production. The latter is expected to be approved soon.
The new tariff will be added to the one approved last July , which affected nearly a hundred countries, including EU members, for allegedly violating forced labor import rules. However, it is being challenged in court.
The federal administration has not disclosed how much the new customs duties will amount to, but they will be similar to those Trump set earlier last year. In any case, they will not exceed the levels set in trade agreements and will be applied specifically to each economy, rather than imposed as a general rate, according to Bloomberg.
It is expected that countries and blocs that signed trade agreements with the United States, such as Japan or the EU, will receive special treatment so that the new tariff complies with the agreements. It is therefore anticipated that tariffs will be 15% or less. Other countries, however, would be set higher tariffs.
China could receive a higher tariff, as the Trump Administration has emphasized that its production subsidies are widespread and particularly harmful to the global economy. Moreover, this would counter criticism arising from the Nvidia case that the White House has been too lenient with China.

articles.title_orig: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state
articles.title_zh: Utah drops criminal charges against Kalshi founders after company suspended operations in state
articles.content_orig:
Utah on Tuesday dismissed criminal charges against Kalshi and its two co-founders following the decision by the prediction market platform on Monday to suspend operations in the state.
The state originally filed the 14 criminal charges against the company and founders Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara on Oct. 28, claiming that Kalshi operated an illegal gambling operation in the state.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission — the federal regulator for prediction markets which views itself as the sole body that can develop rules over the growing industry — sued Utah the day before the state announced its charges.
Mansour and Lara were slated to appear in a Utah district court on Dec. 4, according to court documents.
However, Kalshi suspended operations in Utah on Monday, citing legal uncertainty. Utah Attorney General Derek Brown celebrated the decision in a statement announcing the move to dismiss the state's charges.
"Every company in this space should take note," he said. "If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable."
Brown's office noted in the statement that dismissal is without prejudice, meaning if Kalshi were to begin operations again in the state the charges could be refiled.
"Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized," Kalshi's general counsel Yaakov Roth said in a post on X . "We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets."
While Kalshi faces legal setbacks in Utah, it faced some relief in New York on Monday when a state judge denied an emergency temporary restraining order against the company to halt its operations in the jurisdiction . The court will hear arguments on the matter again in January.
Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

articles.title_orig: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.title_zh: Zelenskiy confirms Ukraine hit Russian ship in Gulf of Finland, ally Norway urges caution
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo ship struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland has left Finnish territorial waters after posing a “serious danger” there, according to Finland’s President Alexander Stubb.
Stubb said late on Sunday that Finland would continue working to maintain stability and security in the Gulf of Finland and thanked the authorities for their response to Saturday’s incident.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it was previously anchored. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
A fire aboard the Sparta II continued to burn through the night despite efforts to extinguish it, the Finnish coastguard said.
“Unfortunately, the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression are also visible in our region,” Stubb said on X.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week that it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to United States sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Is Falling Again. Why the Jensen Jubilation Is Already Fading.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Is Falling Again. Why the Jensen Jubilation Is Already Fading.
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: GTA 6 Cloud Streaming Comes To PS5 And PlayStation Portal
articles.title_zh: GTA 6 Cloud Streaming Comes To PS5 And PlayStation Portal
articles.content_orig:
You no longer need to free up 212GB on your PS5 for Rockstar’s blockbuster.
You now have even more ways to play Grand Theft Auto 6 . As spotted by a ResetEra user, if you're a PlayStation Plus Premium subscriber and you buy a copy of the game, you can stream it to a PlayStation 5 or PlayStation Portal. That means you won't need to set aside 212GB of precious storage space on your console to install GTA 6 . In fact, you won't necessarily need a PS5 at all to play GTA 6. A PlayStation Portal will do the trick.
The PlayStation Store page for the game now states that "PS5 and PS Portal cloud streaming [is] supported only with Premium subscription." I bought GTA 6 on a separate account from the one that my PS Plus subscription is on, so I haven't been able to test it yet, unfortunately.
A report last month suggested Xbox would have exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6 . However, Xbox Chief Strategy Officer Matthew Ball clarified that wasn't the case .
Much like with Xbox Cloud Gaming, it doesn't seem that there's a way for PlayStation users to stream their copy of GTA 6 to PC via the cloud. Remote play from your console to PC still works (I forgot about that option and it's about to destroy my productivity).
The maker of Asobi, a third-party app that supported PS Plus Premium streaming, said last week Sony was blocking its connections to stream PS5 games from the service. Cloud versions of PS3 and PS4 titles and remote play from a PS5 console still work on Asobi. Sony is also shutting down its own PlayStation Plus app for PC next month because barely anyone was using it, but that's mainly for PS3 and PS4 games anyway.
It's perhaps worth noting that PS Plus Premium will stream GTA 6 at PS5 quality. The Xbox Cloud Gaming streams are limited to Xbox Series S graphics settings . Xbox Cloud Gaming also has time limits as of this month, while PS Plus Premium does not.
Sony announced on Monday that GTA 6 was the biggest game release in the platform's history . More than 39 million unique players explored Leonida on PS5 on the game's first weekend, logging 683 million hours of total gameplay. Developer Rockstar Games said it sold 32.5 million pre-orders of GTA 6 , generating $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales.
A PC version of GTA 6 is all but certainly on the way, perhaps as soon as early next year . Efforts are underway to recompile the leaked Xbox build for PC as well.

articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Today's big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire?
CoreWeave stock rose 22.3% on Monday, November 23, 2026. The S&P 500 gained 4.7% the same session. There was no earnings report or SEC filing from the company around the move. The gain came the day Nvidia 's board reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive.
Investors saw cloud companies that borrowed money to buy Nvidia's chips as among the biggest winners from his return. CoreWeave and Oracle were two of them, and both stocks rose sharply that day.
CoreWeave owed $66.2 billion at the end of September 2026. At Monday's close, that debt was 245.1% of its stock market value. For the S&P 500 as a whole, debt is 20.2% of stock market value.
CoreWeave owes more than twice what its shares are worth, and its stock fell 12% on Friday before Monday's gain. Drops that size are hard to sit through when your savings have to cover the bills. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500's, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays .
On its November 10 earnings call, management said it expects to fund most of the remaining capital spending needed to deliver its order backlog with loans tied to specific customer contracts. For more on its borrowing, see Why CoreWeave Can't Pay Down Debt From Its Cash .
CoreWeave rose with its group, but much further. Its sub-industry is systems software. The 29 other companies in it worth $2 billion or more had a median gain of 5.6%. Of those, 28 rose and 1 fell. In all, 18 of them gained five percent or more.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.title_zh: Kalshi makes “difficult decision” to halt Utah trading after losing court fights
articles.content_orig:
Kalshi made the “difficult decision” to pause operations in Utah after losing a court fight to block the state’s ongoing enforcement actions under Utah gambling laws, Kalshi spokesperson Jacki McGavick said Monday.
It seems Kalshi’s legal troubles in Utah have become too much for the prediction market platform to gamble on continued operations there. In Utah, several lawsuits are still playing out, and Kalshi also lost a bid to persuade a federal appeals court to block those cases until the appeal is resolved.
Kalshi also wasn’t saved by an emergency motion from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission—which argues that the CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over prediction market trading. At this time, the federal district court has not granted that motion to block Utah’s enforcement actions, either.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi,” McGavick said. “We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated.”
Utah’s attorney general, Derek Brown, had filed both civil and criminal charges against Kalshi , as he defended the state’s 130-year ban on gambling.
In a press release discussing the initial lawsuit, he accused Kalshi of running “an online casino” that violates the state’s constitution. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution,” Brown said. “For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Late Monday, a major Utah-area news outlet, KSL.com, reported that Brown was prepared to jail Kalshi’s co-founders, who had been summoned to be booked on 14 charges on December 5. He defended those plans, saying, “There is a question I have seen from people asking, ‘Well, do we modify this booking process if someone is a very wealthy and well-known tech billionaire?’ and the answer is ‘No, the process is the process; we don’t modify it based on who you are.’”
However, on Tuesday, Utah decided to drop the criminal charges against Kalshi, McGavick confirmed to Ars. In a statement on X, Kalshi general counsel Yaakov Roth said, “We are pleased that Utah has chosen to dismiss criminal charges against Kalshi, while proceeding with civil litigation. Good faith jurisdictional disagreements should never be criminalized. We stand ready to work with State AGs on reasonable interim measures until courts resolve the dispute over who regulates prediction markets.”
In a press release , Brown explained that the charges were dropped specifically due to the pause.
“Kalshi said it would geofence Utah, which blocks access to its site in the state,” the press release said. “The company also committed to monitor for Utah-based IP addresses trying to reach its site. The Office then reevaluated its position and moved to dismiss the criminal case against the company and the individual defendants.”
Brown threatened that the charges would be raised again if Kalshi tried to renew operations.
“Utah does not allow gambling, and prediction markets are gambling,” Brown said. Kalshi has pulled out of Utah, and if it returns, so will the charges. Every company in this space should take note. If they promote, support, or enable gambling, we will hold them accountable.”
Discussion of the Kalshi pause in a Utah sub-Reddit found some Redditors skeptical of the state’s cases as potentially overreaching.
However, many top commenters seemed pleased with the enforcement efforts, suggesting that Utah may have bipartisan support among some residents. One commenter cheered on the attorney general’s efforts as “the one item in the Utah GOP’s agenda I can get behind,” while another agreed that “prediction markets are incredibly toxic and are manipulated against ordinary people.”
Many complained that Kalshi ads flooded their social media feeds. Some suggested the state should focus on banning advertising of prediction markets, while potentially still allowing adults to trade on event contracts if they want to throw their “money away.”
Fears of insider trading were also raised. One commenter laid out why prediction markets seem suspiciously designed to promote insider trading and other market manipulation:
“I’m pretty libertarian and hate banning things. But gambling and prediction markets are a scourge. Even the term ‘prediction market’ is a misnomer. Because ultimately when people with big dollars get involved it creates a financial incentive for them to make fucked up things happen in the real world. Think about it, decades ago we understood that sports betting was a problem because it corrupted sports—s omething that ultimately is pretty meaningless. Then we got all these people betting on the stock market with puts and it created huge incentives to cause havoc with markets. Now if people are betting big money on politics and wars and everything else, it just means people with influence can make money by making improbable/unexpected things happen.”
One commenter joked, “I wonder how Kashi would have reacted if the judge in charge of their case had ‘traded’ $500,000 on the event of them losing the case. Not a problem at all, right?”
On the same day Kalshi announced its temporary pause in Utah, a judge rejected a request from New York Attorney General Letitia James to immediately shut down Kalshi in that state, Courthouse News reported .
New York Supreme Court Justice Melissa Crane said she was “uncomfortable” granting the temporary restraining order so early in the case because “there does seem to be an indication that there would be market disruption that I’m concerned about.” Kalshi attorney Grant Mainland described it a little differently, claiming that a sudden halt would cause a “market emergency.”
“I think this is the ultimate relief in the case, which is improper for me to do without full briefing,” Crane said. Instead of granting James’ request, she recommended that Kalshi take steps to address the state’s top concerns by considering “safeguards for users between 18 and 20,” who are under the state’s legal gambling age, Courthouse News reported.
According to Kalshi’s estimates, New York’s Kalshi user base (1.5 million) is much larger than Utah’s, so the market disruption from the Utah shutdown may not have carried the same dire stakes for Kalshi or its broader user base.
The CFTC has sought to intervene in that case, too, and it seems clear that Kalshi expects the questions of who can regulate prediction markets and what trading qualifies as a “bet” to reach the Supreme Court. Kalshi’s spokesperson did not respond to Ars’ questions on how the Utah pause broadly impacted users or the platform.
So far, “three federal appeals courts have ruled that states can regulate prediction markets, while a fourth found they cannot,” Courthouse News reported. But despite the current balance tipping toward allowing states to regulate prediction markets, Kalshi appears confident that the Supreme Court will resolve the disparate court rulings in its favor.
In a lawsuit filed by a disgruntled Kalshi user, Kalshi argued that it would waste lower courts’ time to continue litigating these cases and that no case should be resolved until the Supreme Court weighs in.
In that case, Kalshi user Scott Bright alleged that he lost more than $300,000 on sports bets that were technically illegal in Washington.
According to Kalshi, all of Bright’s claims rest “on the premise that state gambling laws reach KalshiEX’s federally regulated exchange—the question now before the Supreme Court. Plaintiff puts the cart before the horse; Defendants ask only that the Court let that threshold question be resolved first.”
The court has yet to address Kalshi’s request to stay the case, but Bright has argued that Kalshi is trying to “sideline a case governed by binding Ninth Circuit precedent so that they can wait for a Supreme Court decision that may never come.”
Kalshi did not respond to Ars’

Veteran Washington Post journalist Bob Woodward has revealed the worst qualities of American presidents that he’s covered — and gave just two words for Joe Biden .
The 83-year-old, whose reporting helped expose the Watergate scandal , has released a new book, “Secrets: A Reporter's Memoir,” which chronicles his decades covering Washington’s power brokers.
The 592-page book, released Tuesday, names some of the confidential sources Woodward relied on. Most have died, and others gave him permission to identify them. They include Hillary Clinton , the late Senator Lindsey Graham and former CIA Director William Casey.
While promoting the book, Woodward sat down with Axios co-founder Mike Allen, who launched into a rapid-fire round, asking him to name the “fatal flaw” of each president he has covered.
Asked about Biden, the longtime reporter said: “I only interviewed him when he was vice president.” Pressed for his fatal flaw, he said: “Being president.”
Woodward, who has written two dozen books, has criticized Biden sharply at times. After Biden's June 2024 debate against Donald Trump, he likened the Democrat's performance to a “political hydrogen bomb” and said calls for him to step aside would be “inevitable.” One month later, Biden announced he would not run for re-election.
The longtime Washington Post reporter was more expansive about the other presidents.
He called President Donald Trump a “liar” with “no sense of the obligations he has to the people.” He also said Trump has offered “no justification” for the Iran war.
On Barack Obama, Woodward said he “knew how to keep the shield up.” He recalled Obama jokingly asking whether he had ever thought about becoming CIA director.
Gerald Ford “got it right,” but “it took him a while,” while Ronald Reagan “looks better and better with time.” George H.W. Bush, Woodward said, was the only “one who wouldn't talk to me.”

articles.title_orig: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.title_zh: Trump’s push to restore Nvidia CEO could haunt the company in Congress
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang. She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.
In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.
And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.

articles.title_orig: Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says
articles.title_zh: Trump Account contributions from friends and family pass $1 billion mark, Treasury says
articles.content_orig:
Families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts since the July 4 launch, bringing total deposits to more than $9 billion, the U.S. Department of the Treasury said Tuesday in an announcement exclusively provided to CNBC.
The $1 billion in Trump Account deposits come from more than 3 million individuals, according to the agency. That total does not include the government's seed money or philanthropic gifts from donors such as Michael and Susan Dell .
"The American people are investing in Trump Accounts with a generosity that represents the finest instincts of our national character," U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a written statement.
"Trump Accounts are a transformative government program for American children. It is the largest government start-up in American history," Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano said in the statement.
Also known as 530A accounts, Trump Accounts are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.
Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.
Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.
Most recently, Snowflake chairman Frank Slootman and his wife, Brenda, announced they would give $1,000 to every child in Montana born in 2023 and 2024.
The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations , a move meant to pave the way for more philanthropic gifts, according to Bisignano.
These rules make it more attractive for donors, according to Ben Henry-Moreland, a certified financial planner with advisor platform Kitces.com.
By gifting stocks, wealthy founders and shareholders can avoid the capital gains taxes that would otherwise be triggered by selling appreciated stock and donating the cash proceeds. However, it also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.
The Trump Accounts milestone comes as more billionaires and companies pledge support to the investment account for kids.
In an exclusive interview with CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," Bessent on Nov. 20 announced an Anthropic co-founder would make a "large gift" to Trump Accounts over the next few weeks.
A person briefed on the announcement confirmed that the Anthropic co-founder Bessent referred to is Tom Brown and that it is part of his broader philanthropic plan. The person asked not to be named because the matter is private.
"This is the perfect vehicle to donate to the children of America, and they will receive 100% of the proceeds," Bessent said.
Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which experts say may come via Trump Accounts .
In a separate funding announcement, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell said she would donate around 2 million shares of her and her husband's SpaceX stock to the accounts.
On Monday, Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and an architect of Trump Accounts, told CNBC's " Halftime Report " that more large-scale donations may be in the pipeline.
"I want everybody to own shares of Nvidia , in Anthropic, in OpenAI," he said. "We created 70 million stock accounts — free stock accounts — for every single citizen under the age of 18 to do just that, and we have huge announcements coming."

articles.title_orig: Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note
articles.title_zh: Op-ed: Trump’s Nvidia board intervention put a price on national security. Our adversaries will take note
articles.content_orig:
President Donald J. Trump has accomplished something extraordinary. He directly inserted himself into the boardroom of one of America's most strategically important companies, Nvidia , helping to reverse a corporate leadership decision, and personally vouched for restored CEO Jensen Huang as having a clean bill of health regarding the national security investigations into his business activities with China.
On Monday, after Nvidia's board reinstated Huang following his resignation amid a counterintelligence controversy and allegations that Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, is under suspicion of being a Chinese intelligence asset, Wall Street celebrated with a historic market bounce. But the market's enthusiasm should not obscure a far more consequential question circulating in Washington, D.C.: Does American national security have a price?
What happened at Nvidia raises the frightening possibility that it does, and it fits a recent pattern that is exactly what geopolitical rivals around the world want to see. Consider the economic pressures surrounding the Iran war. Disruptions to energy markets, shipping, supply chains, and consumer prices have complicated American strategic decision-making. These are notably different circumstances, but they raise the same troubling question about the costs of defending American national security interests, and when they become economically unpalatable to those in the Trump administration.
Beijing, Tehran, and Moscow are watching — as are our allies and partners — and they all may agree on one thing: America has an Achilles' heel that military and technological superiority cannot overcome. It is possible to impose sufficient economic pain to alter Washington's strategic calculation with friends and foes alike. Bleed American capital markets, disrupt commerce, squeeze consumers, and eventually Washington may look for an exit.
Despite the narrative that the president is weaving, there is a fundamental difference between responsibly weighing economic consequences and allowing adversaries to conclude that they can impose an economic veto over U.S. national security policy. Trump told CNBC in an extensive interview on Monday morning that when it comes to national security, "losing the brain power of somebody like Jensen ... would be a far bigger threat than anything we're talking about."
"The bigger impact was the long term. The bigger impact was you know he's got other chips in his brain that nobody else knows about, including me, that nobody else understands," Trump said. "This was a big loss. This was a tremendous loss. And you saw that it affected the market. It affected even, I think it even affected the perception of our country in the world," the president said.
And that's true, but not only in the way Trump thinks it did.
This is not about whether Huang is a brilliant executive or whether Nvidia is enormously important to American competitiveness. Both are true. The question that America, particularly its government, must ask is whether Huang's economic importance justifies subordinating corporate governance, interfering with counterintelligence procedures, and stymying national security oversight.
Trump characterized the Justice Department's assessment as having exonerated Huang. Yet Nvidia's board reinstated him while its own review remained open.
The allegations involving reported contacts with Chinese intelligence assets do not establish legal wrongdoing. However, presidential personal assurances are not substitutes for independent counterintelligence assessments and investigations or congressional oversight. Monday's rising stock price might only measure what shareholders believe Huang at the helm of Nvidia is worth, while discounting or ignoring the unresolved counterintelligence risk that Huang may still pose to Nvidia and the entire artificial intelligence ecosystem.
The Trump administration, Silicon Valley, and Wall Street may believe the matter is closed.
"That thing's like a rocket ship going in the wrong direction. Now it's a rocket ship going in the right direction, and it's taking the whole market," Trump told CNBC about Nvidia's 31.5% Monday gains.
One glaring vulnerability still on the horizon is what Washington does not know. If Beijing possesses additional damaging information, it controls whether, when, and how that information might be weaponized in an ongoing and now reignited strategic competition between the U.S. and China. Beijing retains the capacity to reopen this matter at a time of its choosing. Chinese intelligence could drip-feed disclosures, compel repeated explanations from Huang and the president, and transform Monday's declaration of resolution of this matter into a prolonged national security vulnerability.
There is also a striking irony here. Some pundits are comparing Trump's intervention to China's state-controlled market. To be sure, the Chinese government has a very heavy hand in its economy, but one thing the Chinese Communist Party will never do is put an individual ahead of national security and political authority despite the economic impact that this person or company is perceived to have. Xi Jinping and China's Communist Party have demonstrated a willingness to make almost the opposite calculation about national security and economic growth. Under Xi, national and political security generally takes precedence over the interests of individual companies and brilliant executives.
Consider Jack Ma. In 2020, Beijing halted Ant Group's planned $37 billion initial public offering and subsequently imposed sweeping regulatory restrictions on Ma's business empire. Beijing accepted substantial economic consequences to reinforce national security and political authority. This is not an argument for importing China's authoritarian model into American corporate governance. But the strategic asymmetry is noteworthy to revisit in this latest comparative context. Beijing has demonstrated that even its most celebrated entrepreneurs are not indispensable to the party and the nation. Washington risks signaling that some of its entrepreneurs are in fact indispensable to the state, which ironically potentially makes them even bigger intelligence targets for foreign adversaries.
As an economic matter, the commercial realities of Nvidia's China business make this situation even more perplexing. China, including Hong Kong, accounted for just 9.1% of Nvidia's reported global revenue in fiscal 2026, down from 19.2% the previous year. Its latest fourth-quarter guidance assumes no Chinese data center compute revenue. Nvidia did change the way it reports geographic sales, to customer headquarter address, in late 2025. But anyone familiar with Chinese strategic documents, including the 15th Five-Year Plan, should understand that Beijing has no intention of becoming permanently "addicted" to American chips. Its objective is technological self-reliance, not expanding Nvidia's market share and by extension its dependency on them.
Whatever the exact figure, I cannot think of a number that is worth selling out U.S. national security over, but it certainly isn't  9.1%, which is also a number that will continue to shrink. Furthermore, if the AI ecosystem is critical to our economy and our national security, then selling advanced chips to China or loosening export controls is the opposite of what we should be doing because the chips are used to juice the compute of Chinese LLMs that compete with ours, and to increase the effectiveness and lethality of Chinese weapons systems. The questionable sales of Nvidia chips in Asia, which are at the heart of this story, support neither our economy nor our national security. They undermine them both.

articles.title_orig: Venezuela unveils $240bn debt pile ahead of historic restructuring
articles.title_zh: Venezuela unveils $240bn debt pile ahead of historic restructuring
articles.content_orig:
A cargo ship is loaded at the Bolivarian port of La Guaira, in La Guaira, Venezuela, June 18, 2024. REUTERS/Leonardo Fernandez Viloria
By Mayela Armas, Libby George and Rodrigo Campos
CARACAS/LONDON/NEW YORK, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Venezuela's government put its total debt at $237.5 billion in a long-awaited macroeconomic framework published on Tuesday, providing the clearest picture in years of the country's shattered finances and a potential foundation for one of the world's largest-ever debt restructurings.
In power since 1999, Venezuela's socialist government expects economic output to more than double in the next five years, to $200.9 billion, according to the nearly 200-page document.
The oil-rich country has endured more than a decade of economic crisis marked by widespread shortages of basic necessities, power outages and a migrant crisis that has seen millions of people flee its borders.
Chronic mismanagement and US sanctions imposed on the government of former President Nicolas Maduro also left Venezuela increasingly isolated from the international financial system.
The country defaulted on its international bonds in 2017 and remained largely shut out of global capital markets until US forces seized Maduro during a raid in January, opening the way for renewed international engagement. Maduro is being held in US custody on drug trafficking and other charges.
“We have normalized Venezuela’s representation before multilateral and financial organizations, and we are in advanced discussions to resolve the existing arrears with some of them,” Calixto Ortega, the top economic adviser to acting President Delcy Rodriguez, said on state television on Tuesday.
“We will restructure public debt in a comprehensive manner, and four principles guide us in pursuing this objective: sustainability, comprehensiveness, good faith and transparency.”
The government said in the document, which it posted online, that the country's public debt "is in a state of protracted default and is unsustainable, reflecting the constraints imposed by financial sanctions, the decline in hydrocarbon revenues and years of macroeconomic imbalances."
Although Venezuela's debt pile amounted to 242% of GDP at the end of 2025, the country expects oil production, the key driver of government revenue, to rise by 9.1% a year to 2.9 million barrels per day by 2036.
The framework projects oil export revenue of $30.1 billion this year. It estimates net public hydrocarbon revenue, including state-owned oil company PDVSA's net fiscal position, at $12.8 billion in 2026, rising to $18.4 billion by 2031.
The government also said it planned to adopt a "clear and credible" restructuring plan that would involve all creditor groups.
Such a move could ease concerns among investors that the country might pursue a piecemeal restructuring, which could leave bondholders facing bigger losses.
"We are currently reviewing the information made available by the authorities and it would be premature to comment on specifics at this stage," a spokesperson from the International Monetary Fund said.
"Restoring fiscal and debt sustainability are critical objectives for Venezuela's economic stabilization and recovery. Resuming relations allows Venezuela to exercise its rights and fulfil its obligations as an IMF member, including those related to surveillance, capacity development, and access to IMF financial support, consistent with IMF policies," the spokesperson added.
The Venezuela Creditor Committee, a group representing international bondholders, declined to comment.
The document points to at least $35 billion of PDVSA's nonfinancial obligations, as well as part of a $240 million BANDES bank loan, as "intra-public-sector" debt, meaning the headline $237.5 billion in debt is not only owed to external creditors.
The document does not specify how those types of claims would be treated in an eventual restructuring.
Centerview, the financial advisory firm managing Venezuela's restructuring process, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
After the government report, Venezuela's sovereign bonds, as well as those issued by PDVSA, rose between 2.25 and 6.4 cents on the dollar.
The country's eurobond debt totaled $110.1 billion, including $45.9 billion of past-due interest, according to the report. Its debt to China, part of what it owes in bilateral loans, is $16.68 billion, while it owes Russia $5.08 billion, the document showed.
Venezuela announced plans to restructure its debt in May and promised to release key numbers within a month. However, devastating twin earthquakes in June, which rocked the northwestern and central parts of the country and killed at least 6,500 people, further complicated efforts to assess the state of the economy.
Since the seizure of Maduro, Rodriguez, also a socialist, has made attracting international investment a core priority — particularly in the long-neglected but crucial oil and gas sector.
Oil production fell from 2.8 million barrels per day in 2012 to just over 1 million bpd last year.
The country has secured investment pledges from private companies and hosted a string of investor trips, while also overhauling its oil laws to attract capital.
But attracting investment on the scale Venezuela needs will be difficult without resolving its defaulted debt. The government, in its macroeconomic framework, said it was committed to doing so.
"The scale, diversity and legal complexity of these obligations underscore the need for a comprehensive approach to public debt normalization," it said, adding: "Restoring public debt sustainability will require a comprehensive approach anchored in a credible macroeconomic stabilization program and supported by strengthened institutional frameworks."
The country's economy will grow 5% this year, the document said. Inflation is set to rise but will slow in the medium term to an average of 24%.
While the macroeconomic framework provides a clearer picture of the country's finances, investors are still awaiting a comprehensive debt sustainability analysis that will help determine how much Venezuela can afford to repay, based on expected financial flows, reserve accumulation and total debt-servicing costs.
The Venezuelan communications ministry, which handles all press queries for the government, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on when that analysis would be published.
(Reporting by Libby George, Mayela Armas and Rodrigo Campos; additional reporting by Marc Jones; editing by Karin Strohecker, Paul Simao and Cynthia Osterman)

articles.title_orig: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.title_zh: Denmark: Supreme Court backs hardline immigration law against 'non-Westerners'
articles.content_orig:
Denmark's Supreme Court upheld on Monday a controversial law intended to eliminate ethnic enclaves in public housing, or "ghettos," as the government calls them, by giving authorities the ability to limit the number of "non-Western" immigrants and their descendants who can live in any particular housing development.
The court ruled that the eviction in 2022 of residents from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej, a housing development in the city of Helsingør, north of Copenhagen, did not constitute ethnic discrimination.
The Danish law introduced in 2018 is among Europe's most aggressive attempts to force immigrant communities to assimilate and to avoid the evolution of "parallel societies" in the country. It has attracted both international condemnation and admiration from politicians in other countries that seek to emulate Denmark's approach to immigration and integration.
Under the legislation, residential areas with at least 1,000 inhabitants, where more than 50% of residents are immigrants or descendants of immigrants from "non-Western" countries, and which meet certain socioeconomic criteria relating to employment rates, income levels, education attainment, and crime, can be subject to redevelopment requirements.
Housing developments designated as "transformation areas" are required to reduce the proportion of public family housing to no more than 40% by 2030. This can involve demolishing buildings, selling properties to private landlords, or converting them to other forms of housing, resulting in the eviction and relocation of some residents.
Under the law, non-Western countries include all nations outside the European Union, Andorra, Iceland, Liechtenstein, Monaco, Norway, San Marino, Switzerland, United Kingdom, Vatican State, the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand. The classification is based on a person's country of origin rather than their citizenship, which means even Danish citizens born and raised in Denmark can be classified as non-Western if both of their parents immigrated from non-Western countries.
The seven families evicted from Nøjsomhed-Sydvej argued in their case that the distinction between Western and non-Western origins was effectively a proxy for ethnicity, and thus amounts to illegal discrimination based on race. The Supreme Court concluded that the distinction was based on nationality and country of birth rather than ethnicity, however, noting that both categories encompassed a wide range of ethnic groups and that people of the same ethnicity could fall into either category.
The court's ruling followed a decision last December by the European Union's highest court, which found that the Danish legislation could constitute discrimination on the grounds of ethnic origin, but the EU court left it to Denmark's courts to make the final determination.
Anders Svendsen, Chief Legal Officer for Denmark's national tenants' organization, LLO, told CBS News the organization didn't expect the Supreme Court to rule the way it did.
"We were slightly surprised, considering what the EU court had come up with previously last December," he said.
The organization estimates that several thousand homes have been demolished under the legislation already.
"A lot of people are still quite concerned, because they don't know if they're going to be next," Svendsen said. "This regulation has been quite unpopular among the renters in the public sector, but it has been quite popular in the population at large."
The LLO said it recognized the government's desire to promote social cohesion, but it questioned whether demolishing homes and reducing the availability of affordable housing was a proportionate response.
"We disagree, because it sees public housing as a problem to be solved and less public housing is seen as the cure," Svendsen told CBS News.
Joachim B. Olsen, a former Danish lawmaker who is now the opinion editor for the Danish newspaper B.T., was not surprised by Monday's ruling.
"Legislation is thoroughly vetted by the Department of Justice to make sure that it is in accordance with the constitution and Denmark's international obligations before it is presented to parliament," he told CBS News.
Olsen rejected the suggestion that the distinction between Western and non-Western origin was a proxy for race, arguing that it was based on cultural background.
"It is important to understand that the provisions in the 'ghetto law' apply to anyone living in the area designated as a 'ghetto,' no matter ethnicity or citizenship," he said.
Olsen argued that the policy had been broadly successful. According to Danish government figures , the number of neighborhoods officially classified as ghettos fell from 29 in 2018, to five in 2025.
"Incomes in these areas have risen. Employment is up. So is the educational level," he said. "Overall, I would say that positives outnumber the negatives."
Denmark has become a model for some other European governments as they look at ways to tighten immigration restrictions and address public concerns over the integration of immigrant communities.
While demands for tougher immigration policy in many European nations have been driven predominantly by right-wing populist parties, Denmark's restrictive approach has been championed by its center-left Social Democratic Party, led by Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Frederiksen has been outspoken about her desire to preserve Danish culture and her opposition to a concept of multiculturalism in which all cultures are afforded equal standing in the country.
"We are a Danish society, and we form an ethnically Danish indigenous tribe," Frederiksen said last week on the B.T. newspaper's podcast, Borgerlig Tabloid . "Of course, this evolves when new people arrive here. But it is also necessary that, in the future, Denmark still has a strong majority culture."
Britain's government cited Denmark's policies earlier this year as it changed its own rules on people granted asylum in the U.K.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, announcing a new policy in March under which people granted asylum will have that status subject to regular review, said the "reset in Britain's asylum offer" had been "inspired by Denmark's success."
Denmark has also been at the forefront of efforts to establish "return hubs" — deportation centers outside Europe.
Last week, Denmark joined Germany, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands in announcing plans to establish a "return hub" in Rwanda for migrants who have exhausted their legal avenues to remain in Europe, but who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
