articles.title_orig: Nasdaq Resumes Selloff as Nvidia, Anthropic Shares Slump
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq Resumes Selloff as Nvidia, Anthropic Shares Slump
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 7% on Tuesday, reversing from a strong 31% rally on Monday, after the company's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO.
In a statement, the board said it had a series of discussions with Huang and was satisfied with his candor and ability to lead the company. "The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said. Jones will remain the chair of Nvidia's board.
In an interview on Monday, President Trump said he had spoken "directly and indirectly" with the board and "convinced" them to make a deal. Top administration officials also reportedly assured the Nvidia board that Huang wasn't a national security risk and wasn't facing alleged chip-smuggling charges.
"I am honored to return to Nvidia and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution," Huang said in a statement.
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees during an hourlong, companywide meeting, stating that his actions were "not acceptable" and violated Nvidia's code of conduct. Huang also said that he was in therapy.
"I made some terrible mistakes," Huang said, per the Times. "I was unfaithful to Lori, and I hurt my kids, and of course, I hurt all of you."
Huang, however, pushed back against the notion that he was a "tech bro" and above the code of conduct.
He also said his return wasn't the result of the board caving to pressure from President Trump. "That is completely untrue," Huang reportedly said, claiming instead that the board "gathered facts" — including that the DOJ didn't consider him a national security threat — and evaluated whether he deserved a second chance.
Rep. Gregory Meeks, a ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee and New York Democrat, called on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to testify at a public hearing for the House, adding another request for Huang to answer questions on Capitol Hill.
Huang is already scheduled for a transcribed interview with Meeks and the committee chairman, Rep. Brian Mast, next week. Huang is also confirmed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next week.
"Americans deserve answers to the profound questions that are continuing to emerge about NVIDIA and our national security," Meeks wrote. "President Trump's intervention to reinstate Jensen Huang as NVIDIA's CEO raises even more concerning questions about the administration's own role, questions the American people deserve to hear answered in public."
President Trump's full-throated support for Jensen Huang and his reinstatement atop Nvidia ( NVDA ) has not been matched by Republican lawmakers, who say they intend to keep the pressure on the chipmaker.
The objections broadly fall into three categories. A handful of Republicans say it was a mistake to reinstate Huang as CEO. Another group says they have serious concerns and feel that US national security has been compromised. And a third group says simply that they have unanswered questions about the whole affair.
According to a Yahoo Finance tally, a majority of the 13 Republican senators whom Huang will face next week on the Senate Banking Committee have offered at least a promise of tough questions, and two members have even said Huang should not be in the CEO chair.
North Dakota Republican Kevin Cramer recently posted that the legal cloud was "risk enough to not rehire Huang," while Nebraska's Pete Ricketts said his "behavior does not support reinstatement." Both will have time to question Huang.
The hearing will be overseen by Chair Tim Scott of South Carolina, who said in his own statement that national security will be "central to the committee's oversight."
Nvidia's board undermined its claims of independence by reinstating CEO Jensen Huang before investigations into his conduct concluded, investors and corporate governance experts said on Monday.
The decision is striking because the board effectively vouched for Huang's candor and fitness to lead the company before its own investigation was complete, raising doubts ‌about whether directors had sufficient information to make an independent judgment, these people said.
Nvidia said on Monday that after talks with senior US officials, its board "is confident that Mr. Huang's reinstatement poses no ‌national security risk."
… The situation undercuts the board's standing, said New York City Comptroller Mark Levine, who helps manage retirement funds that hold some 5 million Nvidia shares.
"They told us flatly that he would not be coming back. They have done a total 180 without any explanation, or any indication that concerns about ‌legal and other liabilities have been resolved," Levine said in a telephone ⁠interview.
"They have proven they're not independent, and that is the defining quality that we need from any board," he said.
Nvidia stock is bouncing off its session lows, but shares remain down over 7% as the chipmaking giant gives back some of its gains made on Monday.
The broader chip sector faced selling pressure as investors rotated out of tech and assessed the implications of Jensen Huang's return as CEO and the market's massive rally the day before.
A Department of Justice official said that President Trump spoke with Attorney General Todd Blanche over the weekend and that the DOJ had no evidence of any wrongdoing by Jensen Huang or Nvidia.
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump stated that Nvidia asked "for assurance on the national security threat."
"And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot," Trump said Monday.
Seaport Research Partners senior analyst Jay Goldberg weighed on Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, telling Yahoo Finance that it was "probably the least bad option for Nvidia."
Still, he noted, "a lot of the issues that I talked about a month ago before we had all of this drama, still exist, right? There are still real questions about their growth prospects and their reliance on some questionable sales to Asia and their their questionable financing deals across the industry. So I certainly still have a lot of questions."
Watch the interview below:
When it comes to the AI trade, this has been the year of AMD ( AMD ). AMD's stock has sizzled, up 112% year to date compared to an 11.5% drop for its top rival Nvidia.
As Nvidia's ( NVDA ) founder Jensen Huang has been embroiled in scandal and the tech trade has been pressured, AMD shares have hung tough. The stock is down 12.2% over the past month versus a 22% decline for Nvidia.
The biggest question for AMD right now is this: Does Huang's stunning return as CEO of Nvidia mean bad news for AMD in 2027 and beyond?
Pros think AMD will be just fine, for now.
"I don't see how this changes it completely," Moor Insights & Strategy founder Patrick Moorhead said on Sozzi Unleashed . "I was saying early on when Jensen left that nothing changes for 18 months. And the reason is the supply chain is locked, the wafers are locked, data center configurations are locked around Nvidia design. So nothing would change, I think, if Jensen had been removed permanently."
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang. She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.
In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.
And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.

articles.title_orig: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
articles.title_zh: Businesses supporting Ukraine told to 'act now' to protect against Russian sabotage
articles.content_orig:
The UK government has warned that any businesses providing support for Ukraine's armed forces could become a target for Russia, and should "act now" to protect themselves.
An alert issued on Tuesday warned of an increased risk of Russian sabotage attacks such as arson and threats to staff, premises and operations.
Any businesses that are providing support to Ukraine's armed forces, including organisations in the supply chain, have been urged to take extra precautions, both physically and online.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and there has been a recent increase in Russian sabotage attempts against defence related facilities in Europe.
In September, a man appeared in court accused of planning to "torch" UK drone factories on behalf of Russia's intelligence services in an alleged sabotage plot.
Estonia has also accused Moscow of being behind an attempted arson attack at a drone factory last week, and Germany blamed it for a drone attack at Leipzig's airport in August.
The joint alert between MI5's National Protective Security Agency (NPSA) and the Ministry of Defence, has advised businesses to remove unnecessary detail that can be found online, emphasising that hostile reconnaissance usually begins with internet research.
It also suggested that companies install visible protective security measures "such as CCTV, secure entrances and robust access controls" to "deter hostile activity". These security measures should be "actively promoted... without giving away information that could be used to plan an attack".
When it comes to personal security, any staff members - not just those at the top - should "remain alert to their surroundings, avoid predictable routines where practicable, and consider how personal information, movements and behaviours could be used to build a picture of them, their role and their organisation".
Leaders should ensure their staff know how to manage their personal security, and know what to do if they notice anything suspicious or concerning.
The government said it will give closed-door threat briefings to critical national infrastructure and defence sector CEOs in Whitehall on Tuesday and Wednesday.
Gen Sir Richard Barrons, who co-authored last year's Strategic Defence Review, said the latest warning was "significant but not new" and the relevant companies will be "quite savvy" about the risks of cyber attacks.
He told BBC Radio 4's World at One that while there had been a recent "uptick" of these kinds of attacks across Europe, "we are not expecting an epidemic".
"These actions so far are significant but not strategic. They cause disruption, dismay and some damage but they have not reached the level of them being a strategic threat to the security of Europe," Gen Barrons added.
Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has warned that threats from Russia are aimed at deterring the UK's support for Ukraine, which "must not" happen.
Speaking to the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee earlier on Tuesday, Miliband said the threat from Moscow will endure beyond the Ukraine war and reiterated that any peace settlement must not reward Russia.
Security Minister Dan Jarvis said recent sabotage attempts across Europe "demonstrate the seriousness of the threats we face".
Minister for the Armed Forces, Louise Sandher-Jones, added that Russia and other hostile actors "pose a growing threat", while companies have a responsibility to strengthen their security "and help protect Britain".

articles.title_orig: Waymo says recall prompted by 11 new incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes
articles.title_zh: Waymo says recall prompted by 11 new incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes
articles.content_orig:
Alphabet -owned Waymo said Tuesday its new recall of nearly 4,500 self-driving vehicles in the U.S. was prompted by 11 incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes since Oct. 1, including three on a single day this month.
On Friday, Reuters first reported Waymo was issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control. Last week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on U.S. freeways ​after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state.
Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in a filing released Tuesday that three Waymo vehicles entered freeway lanes marked with cones as closed for construction on Nov. 9, just three days after the company "updated the approved scope of operation to reduce exposure to closed freeway lanes."
Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events, adding it is still working ​on the recall remedy.
The California ban, ​which took effect this month, resulted from a series of incidents in which Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said.
In June, Waymo issued a similar recall for nearly 3,900 robotaxis that drove past ramp closure signs into pre-planned freeway construction zones or entered freeway lanes with active construction by driving between cones.
The ‌manual ⁠traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better respond to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a May 8 collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on Nov. 6.
Earlier this month, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous incidents of its robotaxis passing ​stopped school buses.
Separately, NHTSA and the ​National Transportation Safety Board have opened probes after one of Waymo's self-driving vehicles struck a child who ran into a street in Santa Monica, California.

By SYLVIA MORRIS, THIS IS MONEY AND DAILY MAIL SAVINGS EXPERT
Updated: 14:54 EST, 24 November 2026
Savings rates are at their highest level for years - but many of the best deals come from providers you may never have heard of.
It's typically smaller banking names rather than traditional banks and building societies that dominate the top of the best buy tables.
Savers sometimes tell me that they settle for lower rates from brands that they already know.
After all, entrusting a firm with your nest egg takes a huge leap of faith no matter how well-known and established it is.
Opting for one that you know little about can feel a step too far.
That's why I want to reassure you by telling you about some of the key players at the top of the tables and the protections that you have as a saver.
But first, let's look at why it is the little-known players that currently pay the best rates. It's not that there's anything untoward happening - far from it.
The main reason they can typically pay higher rates than traditional banks is the cost of running the business is lower – primarily because there are no branch networks to fund.
Take your pick: There are many unfamiliar names in our savings tables - below, I reveal who they are and what they do with your money
Instead, they operate only through websites or apps or a combination of both.
Some also keep their customer service costs down by only letting you contact them through their app, rather than giving you a phone number.
That means before taking the plunge, it's vital you know how you can contact the bank you're choosing using the method you prefer.
Our independent best buy This is Money savings tables may be packed full of lesser-known names.
But crucially, all accounts mentioned are covered by the industry-wide Financial Services Compensation Scheme (FSCS).
This gives you up to £120,000 worth of cover if things go wrong. This is the case whether you're looking at the smallest provider or the oldest high street bank.
Here's what's behind some of the new names which are driving up rates.
Trading 212* has consistently paid the top rate on its easy access cash Isa , now at 4.9 per cent including a 1.05 percentage point bonus for a year.
Every time another provider has trumped its rate over the last few months, it has raised its rate to remain top of the best buy tables for new savers.
Trading 212 is unusual in that it is not a bank but a 'fintech' company, which basically acts as a money gatherer for big banks.
It offers savings accounts through its app and then deposits your money with UK banks such as Barclays and NatWest.
It makes its money primarily by earning more from the bank than it pays you.
Vida Savings is an online savings brand of Vida Bank Limited.
It pays a top 5.25 per cent on its one-year bond having pushed up its rates for new savers last week.
In the mortgage market for ten years, it launched its first savings account two years ago.
Money deposited with Vida Savings is used to fund residential and buy-to-let mortgages issued through the bank's lending arm.
Ford Money: Cash saved here is used to fund vehicle finance and dealership lending
Ford Money , launched in 2017, has just pushed up its savings rates and now pays 4.34 per cent on both its easy-access online Flexible Saver and Flexible Isa with no bonus or limit on the number of withdrawals you make.
It plays fair by paying all savers the same rate rather than wooing new ones with top rates while paying loyal customers less.
Ford Money is the savings trading name of FCE Bank, a UK Essex-based bank owned by Ford Motor Company.
Savings deposited with Ford Money are used to fund vehicle finance and dealership lending across Europe through its parent bank.
Investec Bank has operated in the UK for some 30 years when it bought Allied Trust Bank.
It is part of Investec plc, which is quoted on the London Stock Exchange.
It increased its fixed rate bonds last week to pay 5.2 per cent for one or two years with a relatively high minimum of £5,000, rather than the usual industry £1,000 or less.
It has also pushed up its fixed rate Isa to a top 5.05 per cent for a year on a minimum £1,000.
Savings deposited with Investec are used to fund specialist business lending, commercial real estate finance, and private client mortgages.
MBNA Savings offers a good one-year fixed rate bond – at 5.1 per cent was top of the best buy tables a couple of weeks ago but has been trumped by Vida Savings's 5.25 per cent.
MBNA is part of the Lloyds Banking Group, so your money ends up with Lloyds and covered by the UK FSCS there.
You need to add all your savings with Lloyds Banking Group, which includes Halifax, Bank of Scotland, Scottish Widows and MBNA, together to make sure you do not breach the £120,000 limit.  That's because you only have one FSCS guarantee of up to £120,000 for each banking brand.
Lloyds bought the credit card company in 2017 and launched its first savings account nearly three years ago.
Zopa Bank has been around since 2020, developed out of the old peer-to-peer lending group. It works through an app with a low minimum investment of just £1.
It might not always offer the very top rates, but they are always competitive.
It currently pays a near-top 5 per cent on its one-year fixed rate Isa with interest paid monthly at 4.88 per cent and added to your account and has recently launched an easy access account with limited withdrawals.
It pays 4.56 per cent including 1.05 per cent on up to £50,000 in your account.
You can make up to three withdrawals a year – if you make any more the rate drops to 2 per cent for the rest of the year.
Deposits are used to fund consumer lending – primarily unsecured personal loans, credit cards, car finance, and point-of-sale retail finance.
Revolut has become a huge name in recent years since launching in 2015 but only received a UK banking licence earlier this year.
It is now offering a best buy 5.25 per cent easy-access rate on balances up to £25,000 for six months, held by the bank directly rather than a partner for the first time.
Revolut uses savings to power its expanding UK retail lending – starting with its newly launched unsecured personal loans.
Castle Trust Bank is offering a 5.25 per cent rate on a one-year fix.
Savings here are used to fund specialist property finance, namely bridging loans and buy-to-let mortgages, alongside point-of-sale retail finance.
Cahoot has an eye-catching 5 per cent easy-access deal, and has for some time. However, it only allows a maximum balance of £3,000.
Cahoot is an offshoot of Santander and shares a banking licence with its parent bank.
Money here is used to fund Santander's residential mortgages, consumer loans, and corporate banking operations.
These three aren't technically banks. Instead, they are Financial Conduct Authority-authorised financial apps.
Each offers best buy savings deals, but money is pooled to big name partner banks.
Chip has a top Isa paying 4.87 per cent. But money is split into banks such as  HSBC, Lloyds, or Barclays.
You'll need to watch out if you already hold accounts with these high-street banks as your £120,000 FSCS limit will be shared between these and money held with them through your Chip account.
Plum has an easy-access at 4.85 per cent. Money is pooled to big banks that use it for their own consumer lending.
Lemfi has a 5 per cent easy-access savings deal. The app was originally built for international money transfers and money saved here is placed into partner bank, ClearBank.
If you want to make the most of your savings, checking the top rates and moving to a better deal is essential, as is using a cash Isa to beat savings tax.
This is Money's best buy savings tables are independently curated by savings expert Sylvia Morris and the This is Money team. We update them daily and feature the top accounts with FSCS protection.
And don't forget to sign up to our free email savings alerts to be the first to hear about new best buy rates.

articles.title_orig: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.title_zh: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.content_orig:
Sheikh Hasina has been living in exile in India since 2024
Bangladesh's former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has said she plans to return home on 16 December, more than two years after a popular uprising forced her from power.
Hasina, who has lived in exile in Delhi since August 2024, has asked the Bangladeshi government to fly her back to Dhaka, her spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid renewed unrest in Bangladesh, where supporters of her Awami League party have staged protests despite a ban on its activities.
But it's unclear how Hasina will return. Last year, a Bangladeshi court sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over a deadly crackdown on student-led protests that ended her 15-year rule . She denies the charges.
Bangladesh's state minister for foreign affairs Humayun Kabir dismissed the prospect of Hasina returning on her own terms.
"Sheikh Hasina will not be able to return to the country as an ordinary commercial passenger; she will be brought back in handcuffs," he told a press briefing on Tuesday.
Kabir also accused Hasina and Delhi of fomenting recent unrest in Bangladesh, alleging that they were backing "terrorist activities" in the country.
India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a ârequest for comment. In April, âthe ministry said it was â examining Bangladesh's request to extradite her and that it wanted to "engage constructively with the new government and further strengthen bilateral ties".
Hasina fled to India on 5 August 2024 as tens of thousands of protesters descended on Dhaka, and crowds stormed her official residence.
What began as student protests against quotas in government jobs turned into a mass uprising against her government following a deadly crackdown on demonstrators. The UN estimates that up to 1,400 people were killed during the unrest.
On Tuesday, Hasina's spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali accused Bangladeshi authorities of forcing her into exile in violation of the country's constitution.
"Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on 5 August 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka," he said in a statement.
The choice of date is significant. Bangladesh celebrates Victory Day on 16 December, marking the end of its 1971 war of independence from Pakistan. Hasina's father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led the country's independence movement.
Abu Obaidha Arin, an aide to Hasina, described her decision as "deeply symbolic". "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people," he said, expressing confidence that she would once again lead Bangladesh.
Hasina's announcement - and Dhaka's sharp response to it - come at a time when the ousted leader is seeking to reassert her political relevance from exile.
The Awami League was banned from political activities in May last year under the interim government led by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Muhammad Yunus, which took charge after Hasina's ouster.
The party was subsequently barred from contesting February's general election, which brought its long-time rival, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), to power, with Tarique Rahman becoming prime minister.
But the ban has not put an end to street protests by Awami League supporters, who have also called for nationwide shutdowns demanding Hasina's return.
Hasina, meanwhile, has repeatedly spoken of her desire to return to Bangladesh, even as she has acknowledged the risks of doing so.
"I know that they may put me in jail or they may kill me, anything may happen, but still I have to go back," she told a gathering of journalists in Delhi over an audio link in August, on the second anniversary of her ouster.
Hasina's continued political activities from Indian soil have also complicated Delhi's efforts to rebuild ties with Dhaka.
India enjoyed close relations with Hasina during her 15 years in power and had hoped that the election of a new government in Bangladesh would offer an opportunity to reset ties, which deteriorated sharply after her ouster.
But nine months after taking office, Rahman is yet to visit India despite an invitation. He has travelled to China, Japan and Malaysia, and skipped the BRICS summit hosted by India in September.
Discussions over a possible visit in August coincided with anger in Dhaka over Hasina's remarks to journalists in Delhi.
The two countries have since resumed talks about a visit, but no dates have been announced.

articles.title_orig: Putin complains that Ukraine is striking Russian oil refineries despite Trump's request and vows retaliation
articles.title_zh: Putin complains that Ukraine is striking Russian oil refineries despite Trump's request and vows retaliation
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has continued its attacks on Russian oil refineries despite requests from US President Donald Trump to withhold them, Russian President Vladimir Putin has said while threatening retaliation.
Putin made the threat on Tuesday, after Kyiv said it would stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow did the same.
Ukrainian attacks subsided after Trump’s mid-October declaration of an energy ceasefire in the conflict that began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. But they picked up again in late October.
“We see that the Kyiv regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the US president’s appeal and direct request to refrain from such attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice,” Putin told a meeting of government officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin.
“In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.”
He also told the meeting that he wanted additional security measures for energy facilities.
According to estimates from two industry sources cited by the Reuters news agency, Ukrainian drone attacks have cut Russian oil refineries’ combined crude processing volumes by 45 percent since late October.
Several Russian regions have introduced restrictions on retail sales of petrol and diesel following a renewed spate of Ukrainian attacks on oil refineries, according to local media and authorities.
Putin said that while the situation on the domestic fuel market remained difficult, petrol prices have stabilised after they peaked in October.
Elsewhere, Poland on Tuesday accused Moscow of deliberately violating its airspace when a Russian surveillance drone briefly crossed the border.
Reporting from Kyiv, Al Jazeera’s Abdelaziz Mujahid said the incursion “may also signal that the conflict and these confrontations are widening”.
Moscow on Monday accused Estonia, a NATO and European Union member state, of a range of hostile actions “on the verge of triggering open war”, after Estonia announced the closure of their land border.
In other incidents, Warsaw said three Russian Kh-101 missiles landed in Poland on Friday, and a Russian cargo ship with links to the military was hit by drones and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday in an attack claimed by Ukraine.
On Sunday, Ukraine sank a Russian naval corvette in a Libyan port using maritime drones. Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the drone attack was a legitimate act of self-defence, following criticism from Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli.
Additionally, British security officials on Tuesday warned United Kingdom companies providing “material support” for Ukrainian armed forces to brace for Russian sabotage attempts.
Meanwhile, a Russian attack killed two people in the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia overnight, Governor Mykhailo Semikin said on Tuesday.
Forty people, including four children, were wounded in the assault, Semikin added. Images and a video on his Telegram account showed a damaged apartment building with its windows blown out and rubble on the ground.
The Interfax news agency, citing Russia’s Defence Ministry, said on Tuesday that the Russian military hit drone control sites, Starlink satellite terminals and other military assets in Ukraine’s Sumy region, also killing a number of servicemen.

articles.title_orig: As Ukraine sinks Russian ships, some NATO nations voice anxiety over war's spread to new regions
articles.title_zh: As Ukraine sinks Russian ships, some NATO nations voice anxiety over war's spread to new regions
articles.content_orig:
Some NATO countries are voicing increasing anxiety as hostilities in the nearly five-year war sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine spread beyond the two countries' borders.
Polish authorities accused Russia again Tuesday of deliberately violating the nation's airspace as officials said a surveillance drone briefly crossed the Polish border before turning back into Ukraine. Poland, a member of the U.S.-led NATO alliance and a neighbor and close ally of Ukraine, accused Moscow of a deliberate provocation late last week after three Russian missiles landed on Polish soil.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Paweł Zalewski said in a radio interview on Tuesday that the Russian drone crossed the border for a "very short time" and was "monitored from the very beginning."
"I spoke with the Operational Command of the Armed Forces, and the decision was made not to shoot it down, as they did not want to risk any casualties or damage on the civilian side," Zalewski told Radio Poland. "We assume this was an intentional act."
Norway's Defense Minister Tore Sandvik said Tuesday, meanwhile, that the Scandinavian country was speaking with Ukrainian officials about the "need for stability in our near areas," following a strike on Saturday that hit a U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy acknowledged Ukraine had carried out that strike in a social media post on Monday, saying the country's forces used seven domestically produced naval drones to attack the ship.
The Sparta II cargo vessel, which is operated by Russian defense logistics firm Oboronlogistika, has been under U.S. sanctions since 2022 for illicit transportation of military hardware. Russian authorities confirmed that it had been towed back to a Russian port on Tuesday.
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani spoke Tuesday with his Ukrainian counterpart Andriy Sybiha, meanwhile, in a phone call to express Italy's concern over another Ukrainian attack carried out over the weekend, this one off the coast of Libya.
Zelenskyy lauded Ukrainian forces on Monday for that attack, which sank a Russian warship and damaged another U.S.-sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, the MV Angara, off the North African nation's Mediterranean coast, where Russia has a naval base.
"The minister emphasized to his Ukrainian counterpart how crucial it is for Italy to keep working to prevent the conflict with Russia from spreading into the Mediterranean," Italy's Foreign Ministry said Tuesday in a readout of the ministers' call.
Zelenskyy framed the strikes on the Russian ships as legitimate defensive actions in response to Russia's ongoing deadly missile and drone strikes, which it launches from land, sea and air.
"Despite all the enemy's efforts to counter the attack, the Russian corvette Merkury was sunk," Zelenskyy said. "We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia's aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons."
The Russian Foreign Ministry this week accused Estonia, another NATO ally, of being "on the verge of triggering open war" after the small Baltic country announced it would close its land border with Russia starting Dec. 1.
Estonia accused Russian intelligence agencies last week of a plot to infiltrate and sabotage the domestic defense company Threod Systems.
"Any attempt to threaten Estonia's security, sow fear, or act hostilely against us will be met with a decisive response," Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said in a statement last week. "By closing the border crossings, we are sending a clear message to the Kremlin: Russia's hostile actions come at a cost. The more aggressively Russia behaves, the narrower its room for manoeuvre becomes."
The Estonian move came only a couple of weeks after Poland's prime minister said a large-scale security operation launched along the Polish-Russian border may have prevented a sabotage or provocation operation by Russian operatives.
While NATO members' concern over the spread of the war has been more clearly iterated in recent weeks, Ben Hodges, a former top commander of the U.S. Army in Europe, told CBS News on Tuesday that, in his opinion, all of Ukraine's actions constitute a legitimate defense in the face of Russia's aggression.
"Ukraine is doing exactly what they need to do to disrupt Russian oil/gas exports and other international activities to degrade Russia's ability to sustain its war effort," Hodges said. "This is also an important signal to anyone who would willingly support Russia's shadow fleet ."
Moscow uses its so-called shadow fleet —   hundreds of dubiously registered tankers — to evade international sanctions on its oil sales, keeping money flowing in to power its war machine.
Hodges told CBS News that Kyiv has likely calculated the risks involved in attacking Russian vessels in neutral waters.
"The risk is that Russia will attempt to use these as an excuse for its attacks against the Ukrainian economy and civilian infrastructure," he told CBS News. "But Ukraine knows this and anticipates it."
"Most European countries also already understand this and will not be moved by it," he added.

articles.title_orig: AG Blanche, FBI’s Patel dodge questions about Jensen Huang investigation
articles.title_zh: AG Blanche, FBI’s Patel dodge questions about Jensen Huang investigation
articles.content_orig:
How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO
US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday if the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."
Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged China spy who led Megaspeed,  a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping to divert advanced chips to China.
In a joint statement last week, the commerce and justice departments said they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But speaking to reporters on Tuesday, Blanche said the latter department has "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.
Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with any efforts to get to the bottom of whether the company or Huang potentially knew about any chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.
"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.
"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."
While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.
Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, chairman of Nvidia's board, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
On Monday, Trump said he spoke to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .
Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.
Republican congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the Administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".
Democratic congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House oversight committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Microsoft declares 'Code Red' after historic outage, internal memos show
articles.content_orig:
By STACY LIBERATORE, US SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY EDITOR and REUTERS
Published: 13:20 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 16:08 EST, 24 November 2026
Microsoft has declared 'Code Red,' its most severe internal alert, to fix serious failures exposed by a 24-hour global outage .
The November 12 through 13 outage hit Outlook, Teams, Copilot and Exchange Online, disrupting governments in Australia, Japan and the US, delaying trading firms and interfering with airline communications.
Microsoft blamed a previously undetected Windows flaw introduced in July and ruled out cyberattacks or AI agents as the cause. Chief executive Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption.
Internal memos reviewed by Reuters revealed that scattered technical information made it difficult for engineers to coordinate their response.
Microsoft executive Amanda Silver described engineers working through a 'fog of war,' exchanging more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats while trying to restore services.
Jason Henderson, president of Microsoft's M365 Core division, told staff that no previous Exchange Online outage had left so many customers without email for so long.
In another memo, Henderson said an urgent fix for a separate incident took five to six days to reach systems worldwide, a process he wants completed within an hour for the most urgent security problems.
Microsoft also wants to resolve future worldwide outages within an hour and plans to use AI agents to help engineers identify technical problems faster.
Microsoft has declared 'Code Red' to fix serious failures exposed by a 24-hour global outage
Microsoft blamed the outage on a previously undetected Windows flaw introduced in July and ruled out cyberattacks or AI agents as the cause. Chief executive Satya Nadella (pictured) publicly apologized for the disruption
Millions of users around the world began reporting that Outlook was down shortly after 1pm ET, in what experts have dubbed the 'most disruptive email-related business outage of all time.'
More than 17 hours later, users were still unable to open their inboxes, send emails and access other Microsoft services.
More than 430 million people use Microsoft's suite of subscription service apps, though the company has not confirmed exactly how many users are affected by the outage.
It was the most ⁠customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online, Henderson said in a memo to staff on Friday.
This was the first time in the company's history that so many customers were without email, he explained, adding: 'Code Red means that this is the highest priority work for our team.'
Silver issued her memo on Monday, saying Teams chats struggled ​to maintain a cohesive picture of hypotheses and decisions because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems.
During a Code Red review, Charles Lamanna, Microsoft's executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, said the failed component had suffered 'roughly ten years' worth of acceptable failures,' Silver wrote in her memo.
A Microsoft spokesperson told the Daily Mail: 'Our ‌work doesn't ⁠end when service is restored.
Microsoft executive Amanda Silver described engineers working through a 'fog of war,' exchanging more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats while trying to restore services
'Our teams keep working around the clock to quickly implement any lessons learned, and our leadership makes sure this is our top priority.'
Silver outlined five areas of work under Code Red, including reducing pressure on overloaded systems, separating traffic by region and restoring services faster.
Microsoft aims to resolve future global outages within an hour and use AI agents to help engineers identify technical problems more quickly.
Henderson said he would meet daily with leaders of Substrate, the engineering team behind Microsoft 365's core services, and conduct weekly progress reviews to track the improvements.
A Microsoft spokesperson said the company is focused on preventing further disruptions as well as fixing problems when they arise.
'Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday,' Henderson said, adding that he had conducted an extensive review of the broader organizational and structural issues that allowed the failures to occur.
In another memo earlier this month reviewed by ⁠Reuters, Henderson ​said 'urgent patches to our M365 Core services' took too long to deploy worldwide.
'In a ​separate recent incident, an urgent production fix took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. For our most urgent security issues, we need to get from detection to safe worldwide ​deployment in an hour. Needless to say, we aren't here o come.

articles.title_orig: Trump shares meme of Jensen Huang raising red bra in air
articles.title_zh: Trump shares meme of Jensen Huang raising red bra in air
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang is back as the CEO of Nvidia , and is now tasked with selling the company's artificial intelligence vision while also defending himself in Washington.
As Nvidia employees celebrated the return of their leader to the company's headquarters, Huang told the gathered crowd, "I'll be a better CEO the second time around."
Huang will need to be a better CEO to head off the issues surrounding Nvidia and the broader AI industry exposed by Huang's exit. The challenges include a proliferating roster of investigations and hearings from Congress, regulators and state-level officials , as well as technical and competitive questions about how long Nvidia's currently dominant graphics processing units can remain on top.
"There's nothing prohibiting him from doing what he does on his day job," said Katten chair and former federal prosecutor Gil Soffer. But investigations take significant prep time, Soffer said. "You don't just walk in cold."
At Nvidia's GTC conference in Washington, D.C., next week, the company will attempt to convince customers, partners and suppliers that it is developing the future of AI. At the same time, lawmakers will be pressing its newly reinstated CEO over what he knew and when about Megaspeed executive Alice Huang .
Huang, before his scandals, was scheduled to give the GTC DC keynote speech on Dec. 1 to discuss new Nvidia products and the trajectory of the AI ecosystem. In the past, the two-hour speech was the highlight of the event with hordes of fans full of the Huang-inspired "Jensanity."
"People will want to see that it's business as usual, which hopefully for Nvidia shareholders will mean that Jensen Huang announces some new exciting products," said Babson College associate professor Peter Cohan.
Right now, Nvidia has Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, filling the slot. A representative for Nvidia declined to answer multiple questions about whether Huang would appear at the company's event.
On the same day, Huang is scheduled to speak with three House committees — Foreign Affairs, Select Committee on the CCP, and the Select Committee on Intelligence — behind closed doors, where his interview will be transcribed.
"The NVIDIA board's brief internal investigation and reinstatement of Jensen Huang do not erase the national security threats and questions that must be addressed," the chairs said in a joint statement. They said that Huang has confirmed he will appear for the transcribed interview on Dec. 1.
Next Tuesday's interviews are just the first of a slew of investigations.
On Dec. 3, just as Nvidia's conference is wrapping up, the Senate Banking Committee will hold a hearing titled "Protecting America's AI Advantage: Oversight of U.S. Export Controls." Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., who chairs the committee, said Huang will publicly testify as the sole witness.
California's attorney general is also investigating Huang's remarks, and politicians from the Senate Finance, Intelligence, and Foreign Relations committees have inquired about the scandal. In the House, Energy and Commerce has requested a company briefing from Nvidia, in addition to the three committees mentioned earlier. That's not counting an investigation from the Department of Justice and a reported investigation from the Securities and Exchange Commission .
Plus, Huang still has to cooperate with an investigation from the board of directors, led by the law firm Wachtell Lipton.
Meanwhile, Nvidia needs Huang to reassure investors and the broader AI ecosystem that the company is developing new products that will be in high demand. Investors had said that while Nvidia's products for the next two years have been fully designed, they were worried that the chipmaker's pace of innovation would slow without Huang.
Nvidia is facing new competition from chips from its biggest customers, including OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Amazon and Microsoft . The companies have been developing their own chips to reduce reliance on Nvidia, as well as to control AI costs.
"There was already this worry that we're spending too much on it," said Stephanie Balaouras, vice president of group research at Forrester. "One of those cost management strategies is to match ... the workload requirements to the right infrastructure. You don't need to put everything on a Nvidia GPU."
Many in the AI industry see Huang as one of the staunchest defenders of "open-source" AI that is free to use for commercial purposes, as compared with "frontier models" from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, which charge users by the token.
Nvidia has also been spending heavily to develop its own open-source models called Nemotron. Currently, Nvidia Vice President Kari Briski is scheduled to present new Nemotron technology at GTC.
On Monday, Nvidia's board said that "senior levels" of the U.S. government provided input on Huang's potential national security risk. President Donald Trump told CNBC that he was central to convincing Nvidia's board to reinstate Huang and said he gave the board assurances.
Trump's help could draw even more scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers, who were already focused on probing Nvidia's chip sales.
"Today's news that Donald Trump engineered the rehiring of Jensen Huang at Nvidia is Exhibit A about the political corruption and rot at the heart of the Trump administration's big tech and AI policy," said Democratic Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland in a call with reporters Monday.
Republicans have also criticized Huang's return as the focus on the company's China sales intensifies. Still, the investigations could start to weigh on Nvidia's CEO, experts say.
"How could he possibly do the job?" Jeff Sonnenfeld , senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, told CNBC, citing Senate investigations, House investigations and other state investigations, even before Democrats take over next year.
And the reaction in Washington to Huang's scandal could start to affect Nvidia's sales.
Last week, the Department of Commerce announced that it will prevent Chinese companies from getting around export controls by renting Nvidia's chips across borders. On Monday, Commerce also added Megaspeed to a trade blacklist.
And it's not just Nvidia that is relying on a strong performance from Huang. The company's investors, customers, partners and shareholders will also look to see if Nvidia still wants to be at the center of the AI ecosystem. Before Huang was removed, he pushed Nvidia to invest in AI startups, while selling them products, and helping finance their infrastructure.
Remarks from Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress last week while she was interim CEO suggested that Nvidia would be taking a "very strong look" at using its balance sheet to support the AI ecosystem, but it's unclear if Huang's second stint as CEO will continue with his prior showmanship or abide by a more measured approach.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.title_zh: Nvidia CEO Faces Senate Scrutiny Over China Chip and Spy Scandal
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of AI tech giant Nvidia effective immediately following a scandal involving an alleged spy, the company's board of directors announced Thursday.
The decision came amid an investigation into Huang's affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect was spying for China. President Trump said this week the FBI is investigating romantic and business ties between Huang and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang. The two aren't related.
Nvidia's board had been preparing to oust Huang , two sources familiar with the matter confirmed to CBS News on Wednesday night, plans that were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.
Huang's departure also follows a New York Times report Wednesday that five employees at Nvidia came forward alleging Huang was romantically involved with a subordinate, Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare.
The Times also reported Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were caught on video being affectionate at a conference in March, according to two Nvidia employees. The Times has not seen the video and CBS News has not verified the report.
After Huang's resignation was announced Thursday, the Reuters news agency reported that Huang also had an intimate relationship with a second employee, according to two people familiar with the matter. The agency only identified the employee as a woman.
The company's interim CEO will be Colette Kress, who is currently Nvidia's chief financial officer and will continue in that role.
"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Harvey Jones, who was announced as the company's first board chair, said in a statement.
Kress has been Nvidia's CFO since she joined the company in 2013. She previously worked in finance roles at tech companies like Cisco and Microsoft for nearly 25 years.
Nvidia was co-founded by Huang in 1993. It became one of the most valuable companies in the world by designing the powerful semiconductors that fuel many of the world's leading AI firms, making its technology highly sensitive and subject to export controls limiting sales to China.
Nvidia's stock plunged as news emerged of the company's turmoil, potentially erasing almost $500 billion in value. In Thursday's trading, the stock price closed down 4.3% at $166.19.
Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was an executive at Megaspeed International , a Singapore-based data center company whose website touts its partnership with Nvidia.
Megaspeed grew with the help of access to Nvidia's restricted AI computer chips. According to U.S. investigators, Alice Huang was able to gain access to 240,000 chips that were banned from being exported to China. Megaspeed is under investigation in the U.S. and Singapore for allegedly smuggling those chips into China.
In Washington, top Democrats on Capitol Hill have expressed concerns over whether Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang may have compromised U.S. national security.
Following Jensen Huang's resignation, Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts said his departure doesn't absolve him or the company from the scandal.
"Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Warren said in a statement.
Before Huang resigned, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., told CBS News the departure could help China in the competition between Beijing and the U.S.
"With him out as CEO, China could significantly narrow the gap versus the U.S.," Ives said. He added: "The problem now is that there's no replacement for Jensen. It's a black eye moment for him, for Nvidia, and actually the U.S. tech industry. I'd say it's dark day for, you know, U.S. technology."
Following Thursday morning's announcement, Mr. Trump said on his Truth Social platform that there was "only one man" who could replace Huang: former Apple CEO Tim Cook .
Mr. Trump had a close relationship with Huang, who has attended AI-focused White House events and traveled with Mr. Trump to China. Late last year, Mr. Trump granted Nvidia the right to sell advanced H200 chips to "approved customers" in China, with the U.S. government getting a 25% cut — a major coup for Huang, who has long sought to sell more technology to the Chinese market. The deal did not cover Nvidia's even more advanced Blackwell and Rubin systems.
In a radio interview Thursday, Mr. Trump brought up that he gave Huang a National Medal of Science earlier this year. "What a horrible thing that is," he said of the situation involving Huang, adding, "That's so sad to see that happen."
In a statement accompanying her appointment as interim CEO, Kress said that the company's focus will be on "serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders."
"NVIDIA's strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years," Kress said.
The board said it will be conducting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates.
Isabel  Vincent , Jennifer  Jacobs , Aimee  Picchi and Jo Ling  Kent contributed to this report.

The U.S. trade representative's office is set to unveil its latest tariff plans Tuesday night.
The Trump administration will propose new tariff hikes Tuesday night on the European Union, China, Mexico, Japan and 12 other trading partners, a major step towards recreating the president’s global duties the Supreme Court struck down in February.
According to one person with knowledge of the planning, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer will announce the new tariff proposals as part of a report into the countries’ excess manufacturing capacity. The findings are the product of a trade investigation Greer’s office launched in March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows the U.S. trade representative to impose tariffs in response to unfair trade practices.
Three other people briefed by the administration on the investigation confirmed the report was in the process of being finalized and the results would be announced as soon as today. They were granted anonymity to share details of policy plans that are not yet public.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the announcement was coming.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.title_zh: Trump’s intervention on Huang will exact ‘heavy cost’ on rule of law, national security: WSJ editorial board
articles.content_orig:
His accounts continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, according to filings.
President Donald Trump owned at least $12 million in Nvidia stock at the end of 2025, according to his annual financial disclosure report reviewed by ABC News.
His accounts have continued to trade Nvidia in recent months, including more than three dozen trades buying and selling millions of dollars of Nvidia stock this year through September, according to separate filings that disclose trades in his accounts.
The White House continues to maintain that third-party institutions manage Trump's accounts.
"President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognized indexes, such as the Schwab 1000," said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle.
"Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold. All investment decisions are made entirely by independent managers."
Trump has repeatedly vouched for Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang amid the scandal surrounding his alleged afair with a woman U.S. intelligence alleges is a Chinese asset.
On Monday, he took credit for Huang's stunning return to Nvidia , saying in an interview that he spoke "directly and indirectly" to the company's board members about bringing Huang back as CEO.
"I spoke to them. Let me put it this way: And I convinced them. I made the deal," Trump, who had urged Huang's reinstatement publicly, said in a phone interview with CNBC .
Following the announcement, the major stock indexes rebounded sharply on Monday as Nvidia shares closed up more than 30%.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 1,447.98 points, or 3.0%, while the S & P 500 jumped over 4.73%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq soared over 6.5%.
Shares of Nvidia surged, recovering nearly all of the losses suffered since Nov. 12, the day Nvidia announced Huang's resignation .
Nvidia develops the semiconductor chips, systems, and software powering artificial intelligence. In early October 2026, its market valuation reached $5.8 trillion.
Given its significant presence in the stock market, Nvidia is a common holding in many investment portfolios and Trump's shares in the company represent a small portion of his overall portfolio.

articles.title_orig: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.title_zh: CF40 Research: China’s real estate adjustment may be nearing its end—and its external surplus could stop widening
articles.content_orig:
Late last month, CF40 Research , the research arm of the China Finance 40 Forum-a leading non-governmental think tank specializing in economics, shared its annual flagship report, China’s Economy: Toward a New Paradigm—Drivers, Trends, and Policy Implications , at its 2026 Bund Summit .
Guo Kai , President of CF40 Research and a former Chinese central bank official, kindly shared a copy and allowed me to share an excerpt.
The following passages are from the report’s English text. They have been rearranged and intervening material omitted; section headings and this introduction are mine. Corporate debt and profit figures below refer to its sample of A-share-listed companies outside finance and petroleum.
By 2026, the current real estate adjustment may not yet have fully run its course, but signs of structural stabilization have begun to emerge. After five years of deep adjustment, housing sales, investment, inventories, and developers’ balance sheets have entered a new phase, while house-price declines have begun to moderate. Few would expect the real estate sector to return to its former “golden age,” but the drag from the ongoing adjustment on the economy has diminished markedly at the margin. In other words, real estate is gradually shifting from the economy’s largest source of downward pressure toward a more stable influence.
Based on our analysis of international real estate corrections, China’s current real estate adjustment has already been considerable in both duration and magnitude, and the market has likely entered a bottoming phase. Further adjustment remains possible, but another sharp contraction appears unlikely.
Since the start of 2026, China’s real estate market has begun to show signs of “structural stabilization.” We selected 33 core cities for analysis, including the four first-tier cities—Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen—and major second-tier cities such as Hangzhou, Suzhou, Qingdao, Wuhan, and Hefei. We find that house prices, the floor area of new homes sold, and existing-home transaction volumes have all shown signs of stabilizing in these cities. House prices have even risen modestly in a few core cities. By contrast, real estate markets in most third- and fourth-tier cities remain weak. In other words, stabilization is concentrated in core cities rather than broad-based, which is why we refer to it as “structural stabilization.”
Thus, for the 33 core cities, if new starts continue to decline sharply, excess housing inventory could be rapidly reduced, potentially giving way to a shortage. This would provide additional support for house prices and demand and could accelerate the housing market’s recovery.
Over the past few years, the deep adjustment in the real estate market has been the main driver of the widening current account surplus. The underlying mechanism is that the real estate downturn led to a sharp decline in the investment rate, while the saving rate adjusted with a lag. The resulting widening of the saving–investment gap translated directly into a larger current account surplus.
As the real estate market gradually stabilizes, the drag from real estate investment will diminish, while household precautionary saving will stop rising. The saving–investment gap will therefore narrow, and the current account surplus will stabilize at a high level rather than continue to widen. This process bears some resemblance to the decline in China’s current account surplus after 2008, when the RMB 4 trillion stimulus package drove a sharp expansion in domestic investment, significantly narrowing the saving–investment gap.
By contrast, the stabilization of the manufacturing capacity cycle since 2024 has clearly not relied on comparable demand-side stimulus. Instead, the sequence has been “supply adjustment first, followed by a moderate recovery in demand”: a market-driven process in which firms voluntarily slowed investment and retired inefficient capacity in response to weak demand. This differs fundamentally from the post-2016 cyclical reversal driven by a sharp rebound in demand.
According to CF40 research, the new economy’s total value added rose from about 6.1% of GDP in 2018 to 10.4% in 2025, while the corresponding share for real estate fell from 12.7% to 8.4%. By 2025, the new economy’s total value-added share had surpassed that of real estate and had become an important component of GDP.
A defining characteristic of new-economy firms is their greater emphasis on R&D and their ability to generate more operating revenue and profits with less debt. In 2025, new-economy firms accounted for only 11.9% of the total interest-bearing debt of firms in the full sample, compared with 17.8% of total operating revenue and 29.5% of total net profits across the sample. Their share of total R&D expenditure was even higher, at 47.6%. As the new economy accounts for a growing share of China’s economy, the country’s growth model will gradually evolve.
The negative wealth effect of the real estate adjustment is fading, but households’ propensity to consume remains well below its pre-pandemic level, while further improvements in social security and public services are constrained by fiscal pressures. Rather than rising sharply, the consumption rate is therefore more likely to stabilize as the drag from real estate fades. If supportive policies are fully implemented, the consumption rate could gradually rise.
Moreover, the more advanced a manufacturing industry, the lower the share of output going to compensation of employees tends to be. For example, compensation of employees accounts for only 7.8% and 7.6% of gross output in electrical machinery and equipment manufacturing and automobile manufacturing, respectively—two industries that together encompass the “new three.” The corresponding share is 8.7% in computer, communications, and other electronic equipment manufacturing, the industry most closely associated with AI.
On a value-added basis, compensation of employees accounts for 36%, 42%, and 47% in these three industries, respectively, all below the service-sector average. This means that even if the new economy continues to expand rapidly and drive economic growth, households’ share of income in primary distribution will not automatically increase and could even decline. This is because these new-economy industries allocate a smaller share of their output to compensation of employees than the current economy-wide average.
On monetary policy, emphasis should move further away from pursuing credit-volume expansion toward lowering interest rates, improving inflation expectations, and restoring nominal demand. Real estate no longer performs its previous role in credit expansion, while the new economy is relatively less dependent on bank credit. Growth in bank lending and total social financing is therefore increasingly difficult to use on its own as a measure of whether monetary policy is sufficiently accommodative.
One possible aggregate benchmark is that “nominal growth in broad fiscal expenditure should exceed nominal GDP growth.” At present, local governments face multiple constraints, including declining land-related revenues, debt resolution efforts, and rising mandatory spending commitments. Near-term fiscal expansion will therefore need to rely more heavily on the central government.
The new economy has demonstrated China’s capacity to create new productive capacity, but the more important issue for the next stage is how to translate that capacity into household income and final consumption. New-economy firms have high R&D spending, high productivity, and low reliance on debt—an important direction for economic transformation. However, if the industrial structure merely shifts from traditional manufacturing toward more advanced manufacturing, higher productivity will not necessarily translate automatically into a larger household income share or a higher consumption rate.

articles.title_orig: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.title_zh: Yemen’s Houthis Take Second Swipe at Tallest Tower in Saudi Capital
articles.content_orig:
In late October, I met a Yemeni military officer at a high-end mall in Riyadh. He wore a dishdasha and had the gruff, weary manner of an aging career soldier. His unit had been fighting the Houthi militia in southern Yemen, more than 800 miles from the immaculate, marble-floored refuge at the center of the Saudi capital where we ordered coffee.
He was mapping the battlefield on the table with his hands, describing how the latest round of fighting had played out, when cellphones began beeping simultaneously all around us: an incoming-missile warning. Moments later, loud booms echoed through the mall, followed by audible gasps from nearby tables and a child’s cry of fear. Shoppers froze in their tracks, some glancing anxiously toward the glass dome above us.
The Yemeni officer looked at me without speaking. A grim smile played on his lips, as if to say: They are all learning about the Houthis now.
The missiles were intercepted, but the moment stayed with me. A new reality was intruding on a population coddled for years by visions of a frictionless post-oil future, when new technologies would keep everyone happy and entertained.
Saudi Arabia is at war. The Houthis have demonstrated, by means of recurring missile barrages, that they can shut down much of the country’s economy at will. A deadly strike on the main airport in Riyadh killed at least 14 people in mid-October and injured hundreds. More than a month later, few flights have resumed.
“The kingdom today faces the most dangerous crisis in its history,” the Saudi journalist Abdulrahman al-Rashed told a Saudi podcaster last month.
That kind of candor is extremely hard to come by in Saudi Arabia. None of the Saudi or Yemeni officials I met in Riyadh in October would speak with me on the record. They told me that the monarchy is now taking the Houthi threat far more seriously than in the past. Riyadh has struck deals to bring thousands of soldiers from Pakistan and Syria to help defend the country’s border with Yemen. But these efforts may not be enough. The Houthis are building up their forces too, with help from Iran, China, North Korea, and Russia.
Graeme Wood: The only thing the Houthis have done successfully
The Houthis are no longer the rebel upstarts of a decade ago. They are well on their way to becoming the North Korea of the Arab world: an insular, well-armed, and fanatical statelet that poses a threat to the entire region. They have an AI-assisted weapons industry and have studied the Ukraine war; their information operations are way ahead of their Saudi and Yemeni rivals’. The Houthis could soon become more dangerous than Iran, their long-standing patron.
The Saudi military was not designed for this kind of war. The country’s rulers have long been reluctant to build an army that could one day pose a threat to the monarchy. Even now they have dismissed the notion of sending their own troops, apart from elite special forces already deployed in Yemen, to fight the Houthis. But they may soon find that you cannot rely on foreigners when your country is facing a very real threat of invasion.
The current Houthi military offensive began in September, when the group captured the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, on the Red Sea. Saudi Arabia’s leaders believe that this plan was largely devised by Iran. In October, I met with a senior Saudi official who described a strategy coordinated by Tehran and its allies in the “Axis of Resistance” over the past several months. The latest chapter, the official said, began in the spring, when President Trump ordered the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. That left Tehran with limited options to retaliate, so Iranian officials met with their Houthi allies and persuaded them to launch an offensive on the Bab el-Mandeb.
The Iranians, the official said, agreed to help make it happen. A Houthi delegation attended the funeral of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran in July, he told me, and when it returned, the Mahan Air flight that carried it also conveyed a whole team of Axis military technicians and commanders, including two North Koreans, a Syrian who had been part of the Assad regime, and members of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and of Lebanese Hezbollah, the Shiite militia. The plane was loaded with cash and weapons, including drone parts and missile-guidance systems, the Saudi official told me. (Some details of the Mahan Air flight have been reported previously, including the weapons and Iranian officers on board.)
The Saudis had gotten word of the plane’s cargo and bombed the runway of the airport in the Yemeni capital to prevent it from landing. But the flight was diverted to Hodeida, a city on the Red Sea coast that is also under Houthi control, and landed there. Separately, the Saudi official told me, Russia delivered a large shipment of weapons and technology, concealed under thousands of tons of wheat.
If the Saudi official’s account is accurate, it would suggest that the Houthis are receiving more international support than ever. Even if the report was exaggerated for the benefit of an American journalist—Saudi officials are desperate to get more military assistance from the United States—it still points to a larger truth about what the Houthis have become.
The Houthis are the world’s problem. They have proved that they can block a waterway that carries about 15 percent of the world’s trade. They now control about a third of Yemen’s territory and most of its population, and aim to conquer it all. Their use of child soldiers has been well documented for a decade, as has their frequent use of torture, arbitrary detentions, and disappearances. Their rule is rooted in a revolutionary ideology that does not stop at Yemen’s borders and that thrives on constant war. They have challenged Saudi control of Mecca and Medina, Islam’s holiest cities, and they often boast that they will liberate Jerusalem.
Thomas Wright: The price of defeat in Iran
These are not empty ambitions. The Houthis are constantly expanding their missile and drone production, using fiber optics and other materials supplied by China. Evidence recently came to light that they have used the AI tool Claude to improve their guided-missile technology. They have developed pragmatic relationships with al-Qaeda and the al-Shabaab terrorist group, despite sectarian differences (the Houthis adhere to an offshoot of Shiite Islam; the other two groups are Sunni). And, in a show of political dexterity and ideological fervor, they have been recruiting and providing training to ethnic and tribal subgroups throughout the Horn of Africa, in Somalia, Djibouti, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Kenya, and Sudan. These outreaches appear to be modeled on Iran’s efforts to build up regional allies, and could add more tinder to an already volatile region of Africa.
For now, Saudi Arabia lies on the front line of any effort to contain the Houthis’ power. The United States is too deep in its war with Iran to provide anything more than minimal help, and the Europeans are focused on Ukraine. The other Gulf countries have good reasons to fight the Houthis, but for various reasons, they will not.
The Omanis have been hedging their bets for years—allowing the Houthis to smuggle arms across their border with Yemen and providing some intelligence—in case the Houthis end up as the winners. The United Arab Emirates fought the Houthis inside Yemen for years alongside the Saudis, but late last year, long-running tensions between the two countries reached a breaking point, and the Saudis ordered the Emiratis to withdraw. The Emiratis’ absence has damaged the broader war effort.
The Saudis, who have long backed the internationally recognized Yemeni government in Aden, organized a counteroffensive after the Houthis captured the Bab el-Mandeb. They embedded Saudi commandos with Yemeni government forces across the country. Some were killed in a devastating Houthi strike on October 19.
